speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. That statement is uncalled for, unnecessary and absolutely cheap. We table petitions whenever we have a chance. Sometimes they are post dated, if you like, but sometimes we also have difficulty organizing our time.
Members have committees to attend and other things to do. There is no rule that states the petition must be presented the day or day after its certification by the Clerk at the Table.
The Hon. Member knows that we can get difficult as well. If the Member wants to get very difficult, if he wants to play that kind of a game, we will start playing that game, too. I am giving him fair notice right now.

Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time that the Hon. Member has raised this issue. I know that we in the New Democratic Party have received literally thousands of petitions on the trade deal. The importance is that this issue is still before the House and the trade deal will not take effect until next year. Petitions that oppose the trade deal with the United States have been coming in month after month. Until the deal is actually in place, and while there is a shred of hope that the Government will see the wisdom of backing off from this sellout to the United States, we feel an obligation on behalf of our
constituents who have submitted these petitions to raise them, even on a daily basis.
[DOT] (mo)
For the Hon. Member to suggest that there has been any impropriety is wrong and, quite frankly, it is not the way to encourage co-operation in the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under our reform rules the Government has an obligation, for the first time in parliamentary history, to respond to petitions. The Government has had urging from the other side of the House on many occasions to be more prompt in its responses, and I have been working on the Order Paper questions to see that we have quicker responses.
I am anxious to get responses to petitions before the House as quickly as possible because people sign petitions expecting that Parliament, particularly the Government, will listen to their petitions. It puts the Government in a very difficult position when people petition the Government of Canada and believe we should respond, but we do not have the chance to respond until the petition is tabled.
I would point out to Hon. Members that there are two methods to present petitions, first, to rise in the House and present the petition. I can understand that occasionally there are difficulties with committee travel and, therefore, some reason for delay. There is another method of simply presenting petitions to the table, which staff can do on behalf of Members. That is a faster way to bring the petitions to the attention of the Government.
I just indicate to the House that I will do my best to see that petitions are responded to quickly, adequately and thoroughly. However, I need the co-operation of the whole House in presenting them as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the House and Canadians should be reminded about how the process works. First, Members of Parliament receive petitions in their constituency offices, by mail or by a variety of ways. There is a new certification process but there is nothing that says that that certification process must be gone through within a certain number of days after a Member of Parliament receives a petition.
Further, Mr. Speaker, you will know that once the petition is certified, if all Members rose in the House every day we received a certified petition, this whole House would be bogged down doing nothing else but presenting petitions. Indeed, it is

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary has raised a matter which perhaps more properly ought to have been raised on a point of order, not as a part of his tabling of documents. I say this because I am very conscious of the fact that the Hon. Member for Ottawa Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) does pay attention to these rules and would, I think, agree with me, and I hope other Hon. Members would accept that.
The issue is literally that the Government has said, please, those Members presenting petitions, try to get them in as soon after they have been sworn and certified as is possible. There is some merit in the position taken by the Government because people, having signed a petition, now that the rules require that the Government respond to it within so many days, would understandably wonder why there had been a long delay. However, I am certainly not at the moment going to make any kind of ruling on this, except to caution the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary that I think, strictly speaking, those comments at the time they are presented are more properly matters that should be brought up on a particular point of order. I think it would not be appropriate to continue making those remarks.
The Government, of course, has another option, and that is, when sending its responses to those who have made out a petition, it can factually set out when it received the petition and when it replied.
The other side of the coin is that I think it is probably appropriate, and I think the public watching this would think it is probably appropriate-of course, the public realizes there are many hundreds of petitions and Members are not always able to put those petitions in immediately-that there may be very good reason why, in order to have perhaps a more effective impact, Members, using their own good judgment would support the very aim of the petitioners by holding some petitions and bringing them forward collectively. These are all matters of common sense and reason.
I think fundamental to it all is that all Hon. Members ought to try to co-operate as closely as possible with the rules so that the public is confident that the petitions they bring to the House of Commons are answered as quickly as possible. Unless there is further difficulty, I do not think there is any need for further comment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
that Bill C-82, an Act respecting the registration of lobbyists, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when Bill C-82, an Act respecting the registration of lobbyists, was given first reading in the House of Commons on Tuesday, June 30, 1987, that event represented a benchmark in dealing with a subject that had commanded considerable attention over the years. More particularly, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), when introducing this Government's major initiative on public sector ethics in September, 1985, undertook to introduce legislation to monitor lobbying as one element of that package.
In order to ensure that the subject of lobbying was given a thorough airing, the previous Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs tabled a discussion paper entitled "Lobbying and the Registration of Paid Lobbyists" in December, 1985. This paper was referred to the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure under the chairmanship of the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper).
In due course, that committee made its report available to the House in January, 1987, unanimously endorsing the implementation of a registration system for paid lobbyists.
During debate in the House of Commons in February all Parties again supported the concept of a registration system. I
had the privilege of participating and commenting on the committee's excellent work.
The standing committee recorded many of the complexities related to the issue in its report and recommendations. The proposed legislation fully endorses the concepts outlined by the parliamentary committee. I should like to stress that it minimizes the administrative burden on lobbyists and government and provides for fair and reasonable distinctions in treating different types of lobbyists. These distinctions are based on the need to clarify whom lobbyists represent.
"Lobbying" is defined as communicating with a public office holder in an attempt to influence making or amending federal legislation and regulations; developing or changing federal policies or programs; decisions on awarding grants, contributions; and federal appointments to public office. Also included is any attempt by third party paid lobbyists to influence public office holders regarding the awarding of contracts.
The definition of "lobbying" does not include appearances before boards, tribunals, commissions or committees, nor does it include communications with public office holders regarding day-to-day government business or information on government policies and programs.
[ Translation]
The proposed registration system is based on four principles: transparency, clarity, access and simplicity.
Preference is given to a two-tier system in order to keep administrative procedures for the majority of individuals who deal with public office holders to a minimum.

At the same time it permits public scrutiny of those who approach the federal Government and on whose behalf they do so. Where it is clear who a lobbyist represents, for instance, in an employer-employee relationship, the reporting requirements will be simpler.
A professional lobbyist will report under Tier I. A Tier I lobbyist is anyone who under contract to third parties approaches public office holders, even for the purpose of arranging meetings for clients. Tier I lobbyists will be required to provide their name, firm's name and firm's address, the names and addresses of clients, including details of parent and subsidiary companies where applicable, and, for each client, the particular issues to which the lobbying activities relate. This information will be kept in a registry by the Assistant Deputy Registrar General of Canada. Registration must be done within 10 days of the commencement of any lobbying activity. When clients and/or issues change, an update of the information will be required.
Other lobbyists will be included under Tier II. A Tier II lobbyist includes employees and officers of trade organizations, labour federations, professional associations, boards of trade,
March 8, 1988

chambers of commerce, businesses, unions, and voluntary, charitable and interest groups which lobby for their employers as a significant part of their duties. Tier II lobbyists will also be required to register with the Assistant Deputy Registrar General.
However, the demands on them are less onerous. Since it is clear to the public office holder just who such lobbyists represent, they must register only their names and the names of the organizations employing them. The information must be updated and certified annually.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the term lobbyist does not apply to private citizens who communicate with a public office holder on their own behalf, nor does it apply to volunteers who do not receive any remuneration or personal benefit from the agency they represent when lobbying public office holders.

This two tier registration system is based on the well established distinction between the often, perhaps, or possible hidden interests of the clients of third party paid lobbyists, Tier I, and the transparent and well understood interests of corporations, industry associations, public interest groups, and other such organizations whose staff lobby on their behalf, Tier II.
Even among paid employees there are distinctions worthy of recognition. Certain individuals may, on rare occasions, represent the views of their business or association but are not primarily engaged by the employer for the purpose of lobbying. By contrast, many groups and corporations retain fulltime individuals on staff who are responsible for liaison with and communicating ideas and concerns to government. While the latter should be required to register as lobbyists, the former can hardly be considered paid lobbyists.
I should conclude by saying a few words about administration. The administrative responsibility for the registry will rest with the Assistant Deputy Registrar General, reporting annually to the Registrar General.
The Assistant Deputy Registrar General will be able to provide advisory interpretations where it may be unclear if a particular activity could be construed as lobbying subject to registration. All information contained in the registry will be available for public scrutiny. There will be no charge to lobbyists to register, and there will be only a nominal cost to cover photocopying and such, for people seeking information from the system.
Once the legislation is passed, it is expected that there will be a transition period before proclamation. This should allow sufficient time for public education and awareness programs, as well as preparation and gazetting of the necessary regulations and form.
Lobbyists Registration Act
Since this is the first time such legislation will have been implemented in Canada, the Registrar General will table a report to Parliament annually so that a review of the system's effectiveness can be undertaken. Provision has been made for a parliamentary review in three years. It is expected that this period will be required to uncover fully any administrative difficulties or questions of scope.
Since Bill C-82 was tabled I have been pleased to note that the proposed system of lobbyist registration received generally favourable comment from those people who will be expected to register. In fact, so enthusiastic were some groups, they attempted to register forthwith. I think that sort of reaction augurs well for a registry of lobbyists under the Lobbyists Registration Act.
Some of those commenting on Bill C-82 have offered pertinent questions and constructive criticism which have led to the identification of certain areas of the Bill that could be clarified. I am grateful for this input and, as a result, I will be making a number of recommendations in committee with a view to improving the Bill at that stage.
The amendments I have in mind are technical changes. The substantive policy of the Lobbyists Registration Act remain intact.
I sincerely hope that Parliament will give swift but considered passage to this legislation.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to participate on behalf of my Party in the debate on Bill C-82, an Act respecting the registration of lobbyists.
The idea of registering lobbyists is not a novel one. It is not a new one and, of course, it is not something invented by the present Government. Indeed, the United States of America has had lobbying legislation since 1946. In the United States, Table III of the Legislative Reorganization Act, 1946 is entitled "The Registration of Lobbying Act", which of course has essentially been the legislation governing the registration of lobbyists in the U.S.A. Several states of the union also have Bills governing the registration of lobbyists. For example, the State of California has quite stringent rules. As a matter of fact, they were so stringent that we in the parliamentary committee felt that they were too onerous and too costly to operate, notwithstanding the fact that they afforded a considerable amount of transparency.
In Canada the first Bill to register lobbyists was proposed in the House in 1969 by then Member of Parliament, Mr. Barry Mather. On February 26, 1969, Mr. Mather tabled the Bill. He was a member of the New Democratic Party at that time, or was it still the CCF? I am not sure; it was before my day.
The NDP.

He goes back to both.

March 8, 1988
Lobbyists Registration Act

He goes back to both, so I am told. In any case, he tabled that Bill in February, 1969. In October, 1969, at a different session of Parliament, Mr. Mather proposed a second Bill. A third, fourth, fifth, and sixth Bill were proposed by the same Member of Parliament.
In 1974, Ken Robinson, a very distinguished Member of Parliament, proposed a Bill to register lobbyists. Later in 1974, Mr. John Reynolds, a Member of Parliament from British Columbia, proposed a similar Bill in the House.
In 1976, the late, great Hon. Walter Baker from the riding of Nepean-Carleton proposed his Bill in the House of Commons. Mr. Baker, as we all know, proposed a number of such Bills and initiated considerable debate in the House on the issue of the registration of lobbyists.
A number of others were proposed in this House in 1976, 1977, 1978, 1979 and 1980. Finally in 1985 two Bills were proposed, one by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) and one by the former Member for St. John's East, the Hon. James McGrath. Those Bills were basically all the same. In one form or other they would require that paid lobbyists be registered in Canada.
Apart from those legislative initiatives from opposition Members, I think it is important to bring to the attention of the House why we got into this business of talking about registering paid lobbyists. It is not because one Member of the Opposition introduced a private Members' Bill or anything like that.
After the election of 1984, some Canadians decided that they would get into the business of lobbying the Government, which is not abnormal in itself. Lobbying is a profession and it has existed for some time. However, these new people in Ottawa, because there was a new Government, decided to approach the issue of lobbying in a rather different way than had been the case in the past. They decided that they would be higher profile and that they would somehow bend the rules a trifle or bend the practice at least, if not the rules-because, of course there were no rules-in order to get their message across and attract publicity and to be what they considered effective lobbyists, I have a series of newspaper clippings. I just want to read to you, Mr. Speaker, the headlines of some of them:

But he denied any conflict of interest in his own Ottawa lobbying.
"This work is my means of earning a livelihood ... it is my profession and one of which I am proud,"

However, I want to move on to a promise which the Prime Minister made in this House.

Mr. Speaker, you will recall that on September 9, 1985, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) rose in the House of Commons to make a short statement to the effect that Parliament would have a new code of public sector ethics.
One of the components of the code tabled here in the House on September 9, 1985, was the following and I want to quote Section 5 of the new document on public sector ethics tabled in the House on September 9, 1985, which reads as follows:
Lobbying legislation. The fifth component of this comprehensive approach to public sector ethics is the undertaking of this Government to introduce into the House of Commons, at an early date, legislation to monitor lobbying activity and to control the lobbying process by providing a reliable and accurate source of information on the activities of lobbyists.
Listen carefully, Mr. Speaker!
We will require, among other things, paid lobbyists to register and identify their clients. This will enable persons who are approached by unions, and by agents on behalf of foreign governments and other foreign interests, to be clearly aware of who is behind the representation.
I have accordingly asked my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, to prepare, on an urgent basis, legislation to govern lobbying activity.
Mr. Speaker, you may have noticed that on September 9, 1985, the Prime Minister said: "On an urgent basis". It was an urgent and important document, and according to the Prime Minister, the Government had to take immediate action.
I would now like to go on with the Prime Minister's statement, and I quote:
This initiative should not be misinterpreted to mean that this Government is aware of particular improprieties in the conduct of lobbyists or that it considers lobbying to be an inappropriate activity. On the contrary, the practice of lobbying plays an important role in ensuring that governments, in

taking the decisions which affect the lives of all of us, are able to take properly
into account the multitude of diverse interests involved. This Government is
simply saying that something so important should not be shrouded in mystery.
That was the statement the Prime Minister made on September 9, 1985.
What has happened since then? First of all, we have already established that the Government considered the registration of lobbyists to be an urgent matter. Several months later, on December 19, 1985, when Members were still waiting for the Bill on the registration of lobbyists promised by the Prime Minister, on that day, instead of a Bill, a discussion paper entitled: "Lobbying and registration of paid lobbyists" was tabled in the House.
So no Bill on December 19. Instead of a Bill, we were given a discussion paper that was several pages long, plus copies of Bills that had already been tabled in the House, other copies of legislation tabled in the United States, and a paper, in which the author wondered whether Canada really needed a Bill on lobbyists, which identified a number of alternatives, which were either to do nothing at all, ask lobbyists to register themselves, or have the Government legislate their registration. So still no Bill on December 1985.
And then, Mr. Speaker, the discussion paper was shelved for nearly five months. On April 1986, following various scandals and precarious situations to which the Conservative Government had been exposed, the Government decided to order the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure to study the registration of lobbyists.
The committee was charged in April of 1986 with studying the possibility of registering lobbyists, using as background the discussion paper proposed by the Government some months prior.
The committee, under the able chairmanship of the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) and having as its members the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King), the Hon. Member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. McCuish), myself and a few other members who changed around every now and then, started a series of hearings on this issue.
We then went to Washington and to Sacramento, California, to see what kind of legislation they had there. Indeed, we discovered that registering lobbyists was not impossible or pie in the sky, it was a logical thing to do for a Parliament that wanted to have some transparency when knowing who was doing what to whom and at what cost.
Many of the government members who were with us on the trip to Washington and Sacramento were not initially of the opinion that the registration of lobbyists was desirable or even feasible, but after going to Washington some government

Lobbyists Registration Act
members noticed that that great bastion of free enterprise, the United States of America, indeed had a system for registering lobbyists and that this system did not require thousands or even hundreds of civil servants to administer it. The United States Congress deals with some 8,000 lobbyists and the total staff assigned to registering lobbyists and access to that register is composed of some eight people. It is not beyond the reach of this House of Commons to install a system to register lobbyists in Canada.
How many lobbyists are there in Canada? It is difficult to say, because at this time they are not registered. All things being equal, given that there are some 8,000 registered lobbyists in the United States and given that Canada's population is one-tenth of that of the United States, I think it would be fair to say that there are probably 1,000 or so lobbyists in Canada.
The committee did its work, but unfortunately could not complete its agenda before the summer recess of 1986. Hon. Members will recall that in early September of 1986, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wanted to wipe the slate clean and start afresh so he prorogued Parliament and started off with a new Session. The result of that, of course, was that all our committee work theoretically vanished into thin air because the House had been prorogued. However, the Government did reactivate the committee by a motion of the House on November 19, 1986, and the committee got back to work to finish what it had started.
I must say that at the stage the committee was at in November of 1986, there were still a number of differing views held by members of the committee, but everyone compromised a little and we were able to present a report to the House of Commons on January 27, 1987, not simply a majority report or a report proposed by government members but, indeed, a unanimous report recommending the registering of lobbyists in Canada. I have a copy of that report here and I would like to share very briefly some of its contents with Hon. Members.
First, our committee recommended that we adopt a system of registering paid lobbyists in Canada. We recommended further that lobbying be defined and that such definition should be stated as attempting to influence directly or indirectly governmental decisions, whether they be legislative or administrative.
We recommended that the act of lobbying Government be defined to include attempts to influence the making or amending of legislation or regulations, attempting to influence the making or changing of federal policies or programs, attempting to influence federal decisions on the awarding of grants, contracts, contributions or any other similar benefits and attempting to influence federal appointments to boards, commissions and any other public office.
We further recommended that in order to escape the problems which have plagued the United States federal lobbying Act, approaches to influence the executive Members of Parliament including both Members of the House of
Commons and of the Senate and their staffs and the bureaucracy be considered to be activities within the definition of lobbying. The United States legislation is quite old. It was to have been amended at one particular point in the early 1980s, but I believe the Bill died at the conference stage. Unfortunately, that legislation is deficient because in the United States one is not a lobbyist unless one approaches a Member of Congress. The difficulty with that is that Members of Congress are probably very busy, as are Members of Parliament, and sometimes a lobbyist will meet with an executive assistant, a chief of staff or the number two person in the Congressman's office. That, of course, under American law as I understand it, is not considered to be lobbying.
We do not want that kind of deficiency in our legislation. The committee felt that if we are to register lobbyists, the registration should be done in such a way as to include everyone who lobbies the Government for a fee.
Our committee felt we should register only paid lobbyists. If you asked everyone else who lobbies to register, a case could be made that you were impinging upon the democratic rights of Canadians who wish to communicate with their Member of Parliament or Senator. After all, every Canadian lobbies in one way or other when they contact their Member of Parliament to express their view on an issue and to ask that Member to vote one way or other on any given Bill.
Our committee did not want to stop people communicating with their Members of Parliament or Senator from their provinces. Therefore, we felt restricting it to paid lobbyists was a fair compromise. We knew there would probably be some individual who would want to register but could not if they are not paid. However, it was a good a saw-off point at which to determine who was and who was not a lobbyist.
We have been talking briefly about the report presented to Parliament by the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure of January 20, 1987. Time again flew by and it was only on June 30, 1987 that the Government presented Bill C-82 in this House. On September 9, 1985, the Prime Minister said in this House that he would ask his Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) to present the Bill forthwith. One can hardly describe June 30, 1987, as being forthwith. You would think that a Bill which enjoys the support of all Parties would have been proceeded with immediately at second reading stage. Not so. It took eight and a half months before the debate started. This is now March 8, 1988, and we are discussing a Bill promised on an urgent basis on September 9, 1985.
We have talked about the history of the Bill. Perhaps we should briefly discuss what it contains. Again, I want all Members of Parliament to understand that in my opinion this Bill does merit our support.
First, it would register lobbyists in such a way that we will have two tiers of lobbying activity. The Tier I lobbyist that the
March 8, 1988

Minister referred to will be a lobbyist on contract to a client; in other words, a consultant type of person such as Mr. Moores. 1 use his name because I have discussed him earlier, but there are of course many others who do the same kind of work.
This would also include a member of any profession when engaged in lobbying for pay. In other words, if a lawyer decides he wants to do some lobbying, he would have to register. If an engineer says, "I am not really a lobbyist, I am an engineer who does lobbying", that is not good enough. If he is an engineer, lawyer or doctor who does lobbying, he is a lobbyist as far as the Minister's Bill is concerned and I agree with that.
The registry for those people will have information in some detail. However, some detail will be missing. In my opinion, if we required that fees paid to lobbyists be registered as well as their expenses, the Bill would be better. However, perhaps three years from now, when we have a review of the legislation and we see that registering a lobbyist is not that onerous, we could then add that second component. I wish we would do it right now, but in keeping with the unanimous support of this legislation I am prepared to go along with a scheme that will not require registration of fees initially. Reluctantly, I might add, but nevertheless I will go along.
There will also be Tier II lobbyists. They are people who are sometimes the vice-president of communications working for a large corporate entity. In other words, in-house lobbyists. Unions have such people, as do trade organizations, business organizations, voluntary groups and others. They are in-house people who do nothing else but liaise with Government. Perhaps I should reword that and say they work at liaising with Government for a considerable portion of their time. The registry in that case will have very limited information and will not have the same requirements as those for Tier I lobbyists.
The Bill asks that the Assistant Deputy Registrar General be charged with administration of this Act. That is consistent with our committee's recommendation. However, since then we have seen a new initiative proposed by the Prime Minister with respect to conflict of interest. He is suggesting that an officer of this House be appointed as the ethics commissioner or something like that. In my view, the registration of lobbyists should be given to that commissioner, an officer of Parliament, as opposed to a civil servant.
The reason our committee did not recommend that is twofold. First, we did not have the ethics commissioner at the time. Second, we did not want to create a new position in order to register lobbyists. If we are now going to create that new position anyway, then in my opinion we should give the ethics commissioner other things to do besides registering conflict of interest regulations. We should ask that that officer be appointed by Parliament to look after the registration of lobbyists as well.
As I said previously, the Bill has a few weaknesses. It will not deal with fees. In other words, we will not know whether a consultant is, well, shall I say, buying a parliamentarian or a
Lobbyists Registration Act
civil servant an expensive dinner at some real fancy place. Perhaps there is nothing wrong with that, but the public has a right to know who is doing what for whom and how much is being spent doing it.
The Bill also does not prohibit contingency fees. In my opinion that is a major weakness. Right now a lobbyist could go to an individual and say, "Mr. fisherman, if you want to get your fishing licence I will charge you $1,000 for my fee. However, if I am successful, you owe me another $10,000". A lobbyist could do that right now because there are no rules, but even under this Bill contingency fees could be charged. I do not think that is appropriate. In most provincial jurisdictions in Canada contingency fees by lawyers are not permitted. I do not think they should be permitted by lobbyists either.
The Bill does not require that there be a record of official contacts, so that we do not know who was being lobbied. For instance, when a budgetary document of the Government reveals that certain tax concessions have been given to a certain group, no one can go back to the registry to determine who was lobbied in order to effect that particular change. That is a weakness in the Bill.
Another weakness is that the Bill contains no provision to stop someone from registering after having been fined or jailed for making a false statement. Parliament would have no recourse to stop someone who has deliberately flaunted the law proposed by Parliament from registering in the future. The Bill should contain a provision which states that anyone who has committed a certain contravention of the legislation may not register for a certain period of time. It would be similar to disbarring someone who has proven he or she cannot live by the rules.
Some lobbyists stated publicly after the Bill was presented that they do not intend to register. In my opinion, simply allowing such people to register once they decide to do so does not provide enough incentive for people to observe the rules.
The Bill does not include the registration of mass mailings and publicity campaigns. While our committee considered this question and believed such registration would be advisable, it is rather difficult to identify how one would go about doing that. Needless to say, we feel there is a shortcoming in the Bill in this area but we are not sure how to address it.
There are no provisions in the Bill to create an agency to police the legislation in question. It seems little can be done to ensure compliance with the registration of lobbyists legislation. Presumably a person could be fined on summary conviction, but there is no means of policing in the legislation.
These deficiencies are not enough to prevent me from supporting this Bill. I do not want to unduly delay its passage at second reading, but a number of important points had to be made. I am sure that a Bill such as this, which so directly affects the parliamentary privileges of Members, will require

Lobbyists Registration Act
further debate. However, I ask my colleagues on all sides of the House to support this Bill and allow it to go to a parliamentary committee.
I have stated previously that the Bill should be dealt with by a standing committee of the House as opposed to a legislative committee. The Government now agrees with that opinion as well, but the difficulty is that the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure which dealt with this Bill in the past has changed its membership considerably. Since the Members who have expertise in the Bill are no longer members of that committee, I would ask that the Government consider striking a legislative committee.
Perhaps I am speaking out of turn on this particular topic, but I hope the Government asks the Hon. Member for Peace River to be chairman of that committee because he did a very good job as chairman of the Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure.
The Member for Peace River is very knowledgeable in the area of registration of lobbyists. He is also very adept at obtaining a consensus when probably no one else could. I did not believe he could get us on the same side of the issue but somehow managed to do so. I give him credit for that and hope the Government will consider my suggestion.
I hope to have the opportunity to participate on that committee, as well as the Member for Nickel Belt, because I believe that we put forward good suggestions to the House. The fact that the Government adopted a large number of the unanimous recommendations that we proposed in our report is proof that we had some valuable recommendations.
I am pleased that the Minister is finally proceeding with the Bill even though it is much too late. This was a promise the Prime Minister made in the summer of 1985 and reiterated on the floor of the House on September 9, 1985. Nevertheless, it is better late than never and I will be glad when the law is finally in place.
I will be anxiously waiting to see whether or not lobbyists will adhere to these new rules, as I hope and trust the majority of them will. Parliament will be a better place when there is legislation governing lobbyists and we know what kind of lobbying activity is taking place.
Lobbying is an honourable profession. However, transparency is required and should be achieved in some measure with this Bill. Hopefully, three years after its passage transparency will be augmented. In the meantime, let us support this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, we have certainly waited a long time for Bill C-82, which is better known in consulting circles as the Frank Moores bill. In fact, our Party, those on this side of the House, have no problem with the principle of Bill C-82, which is that lobbyists-those who are engaged for pay in persuading, influencing, making representations to elected politicians, the bureaucracy and
their staffs-be registered. We support the principle of the Bill.
In fact, others have promoted that principle, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on August 12, 1984 when campaigning in Kingston, Ontario. He spoke on the question of open Government, saying, "If the Canadian people see fit to give us their trust, we will always give them ours. That means an end to the obsession with secrecy". In another part of the same speech, the man who is now Prime Minister said, "The present Government believes you have only limited rights to know. Conservatives believe you have every right to know". That was pre-September 4, 1984.
The Prime Minister came to power and we do not know what happened to the whole business of the right to know. Somehow it went into recession. It receded into the darkest parts of the Prime Minister's mind. It was completely forgotten, only to be dredged up like some Loch Ness monster from the bottom of the lake, by one Gerry Doucet, Gary Ouellet and Frank Moores, who established themselves as GCI, Government Consultants International. All of this came to light and focused the Prime Minister's mind on what he had said about openness in those pre-September 4 days in Kingston.
It is not a question that Government Ministers do not understand what is involved. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) said that lobbying threatens Parties and that the danger inherent in lobbying is that it gives disproportionate weight to the opinions of the rich and powerful. "How do you explain that in the United States barely half the electorate exercises its right to vote?", the Minister asked.
The Prime Minister before he was elected recognized that the Government should be open and transparent, that it must not only be open and transparent, it must be seen to be open and transparent. But all of this knowledge receded to the back of his mind.
On September 9, 1985, the Prime Minister sent an open letter to Members of Parliament and Senators. He began by saying that it is a great principle of public administration, I could even say an imperative, that to function effectively, the Government and the Public Service of a democracy must have the trust and confidence of the public they serve. In order to reinforce that trust, the Government must be able to provide competent management and, above all, to be guided by the highest standards of conduct.
No one in this House would have refuted or argued with that. He outlined five steps in achieving that goal. Number 5 is entitled "Lobbying Legislation", about which the Prime Minister in his letter to his colleagues said the fifth component of this comprehensive approach to public sector ethics is the undertaking of the Government to introduce into the House of Commons at an early date legislation to monitor lobbying activity and to control the lobbying process by providing a
March 8, 1988

reliable and accurate source of information on the activities of lobbyists. He said that we will require, among other things, paid lobbyists to register and identify their clients.
This will enable persons who are approached by lobbyists for Canadian corporations, associations and unions, and by agents on behalf of foreign governments and other foreign interests, to be clearly aware of who is behind the representation.
No one would quarrel with that. That was on September 9, 1985. We all know that a lot of water has passed under the bridge since then. We had "Frankie baby", the Tory Member of Parliament, the former Premier of Newfoundland, joining GCI and for $2,000 got Mr. U. Snarby his appointment with the then Minister of Fisheries and Oceans so he could get a fishing licence.
We had the spectacle of Mr. Frank Moores sitting on the Board of Directors of Air Canada, appointed by the Prime Minister, and he is lobbying for other airline companies, Wardair and Nordair. He is also representing foreign airline companies, foreign manufacturers of airlines, with Air Canada for Air Canada's purchase of their equipment. That is what was happening.
We now have the spectacle of Mr. Bill Neville who has now formed his own consultant "lobbyist" business. These are the euphemisms we have to learn around here. Any time we see a card which says "GCI Consultants or Susan Murray Consultants", bells start to ring-read "lobbyist" for "consultants". We all know that Billy the kid Neville was close to the Prime Minister and we hear of the role he is playing with respect to Bill C-51 with the tobacco companies.
We know that the Tories have no lock on to this business of an easy movement from Government benches to the lobbyists' benches. The Tories have no monopoly on that. We all know the Liberals did it for years. There were the Sky Shop scandals, with lobbying in the other place for the Sky Shop monopolies at airports. Recently the former Member for Nickel Belt moved very cosily across to the Pharmaceutical Association, representing the multinational pharmaceutical companies for $100,000 a year. She is representing their interests, lobbying with former colleagues and with Ministers. Of course, she took that contract away from GCI, because the pharmaceutical companies had previously hired GCI to do the lobbying on Bill C-22.
We have the spectacle of the former Minister of Defence, the former Member for Nipissing, who is now a lobbyist for the French firm which is trying to sell nuclear submarines to the Tory Government. We have seen the spectacle of Francis Fox, the former Member of the Liberal Cabinet, becoming part of the Frank Moores gang. This is what goes on.
The people of Canada have a right to know who is doing what to whom, when, and for how much. They have a right to know that. If it is happening to them, they ought to at least know who is doing it. It ought to be open and above board.
Lobbyists Registration Act
Certainly a democratic system has more legitimacy when it is open and transparent to the public and when it gives equal access to Canadians. That is really what motivates the desire to register lobbyists.
We have other pieces of legislation which provide the public with information. For example, we have the access to information legislation which is a desire to provide Canadians with information about Government. There is also the Election Expenses Act, under which legislation we may be provided with information respecting who contributes how much to each of the political Parties. The legislation before us is the completion of that system of open and transparent Government.
Abraham Ribicoff, a former Senator of the United States, said the following with respect to registering lobbyists and the role and function which they play. I do not think anyone in the House could say it better than he said it. I want to put his words on the record because they are as true now as they were then. He said:
To protect the democratic process itself and assure public confidence in it, the lobbyist must work in the open. His work must not be cloaked in secrecy. Secrecy inevitably spreads public suspicion. Secrecy helps disguise the voice of a single special interest as the voice of the general public. The stream of letters or mailgrams we all receive may be a spontaneous reflection of the public view, or it may only represent a secretly generated campaign by just one special interest. Congress and the public have a right to know which it is.
I would say that Parliament and Canadians also have a right to know which it is.
We have no difficulties with the principles behind this Bill, none whatsoever. We support the principles behind Bill C-82. We know that scandals and lobbying are not unknown in Canadian history. We are all well aware of that. In this respect we can go back to the Pacific scandal. We can go right back to John A. Macdonald. We can go back through all of the First World War and all the scandals that had to do with the rich and the powerful getting their way. We know that oftentimes the Income Tax Act is drafted in the way in which it is because of lobbying activities by the rich and the powerful.
However, in 1988 we can no longer treat this reality by turning a blind eye to it, as we did in previous years. The time has come to register lobbyists. It is time for lobbyists to come out of the lake. It is time for them to surface. They need air and they must surface. This Bill will go some way to achieving that end.
What does this Bill provide? It provides for the registering of lobbyists basically in two tiers or two levels. This was not the recommendation of the standing committee. The standing committee recommended that all paid lobbyists be registered. We did not simplify lobbyists into two tiers. The Bill before us does that. Lobbyists in the first tier will be those who, like the Frank Moores operation, represent clients directly.

What will lobbyists in the first tier have to divulge? They will have to divulge their name and address, the name and address of the company for which they are doing work, and the particular issue on which they are lobbying. They will not be required to divulge how much they are spending on the lobbying operation. That is the first shortcoming of the Bill.
I say to the Minister that that is an important piece of information that Canadians must know. It indicates the seriousness of this issue to the people involved. If considerable amounts of money are being spent by lobbyists with respect to Bill C-22, then it is a signal to the public of Canada that it is an important issue. The bells should go off in our heads. That is important.
Until Bill C-22 was tabled we did not know all the shenanigans that were going on behind the scenes. Nobody was talking. Even Frank Moores was close-mouthed on this one. They were all close-mouthed in spite of the fact that Gary Ouellet is a first-class magician. He has written 14 books. Did you know that, Mr. Speaker? He has written 14 books on magic. That guy is a lobbyist. This lobbyist has a coat with 14 pockets. It is not multi-coloured but it does have 14 pockets. One can imagine the tricks that one can play with such a coat, especially when one is visiting Parliament Hill. It ought to be required of all lobbyists that they be some sort of amateur magicians. This guy is an expert on the matter. I will come to him later because he is quite interesting.
Do you think that I am joking about the aggressiveness and the extent to which these lobbyists will go, Mr. Speaker? Last May the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) was invited down to Nova Scotia to receive an honorary doctorate degree. This example illustrates the resourcefulness of a good lobbyist. What did Gary Ouellet do? The minute he recognized that the Minister was going down he phoned up a couple who lived down there and asked them if he could use their big house. This couple did not know the Deputy Prime Minister. This guy Ouellet laid on the lobster. He laid on the champagne. He had painters' caps with the words "Doctor Maz" printed on them. He brought in special buddies of the Deputy Prime Minister. The guy who owns the house served the champagne. They ate the lobster. Word has it that the Tories in the local ridings were very upset because they were not invited to the party. The lobbying firm which threw the party is the same firm that represents transport companies and other companies which do business with the Government.

We all know about the lobbying that went on around Bill C-22. I want to tell the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) that it was a neat little trick he turned when he got all the lobbyists to pressure the Government and to use their influence with it.
If we look at the lobbyists who are floating around such as Bill Neville, Gerry Doucet, and Gary Ouellet, one will see that they are all involved with consulting firms known as lobbyists.
They all have their inner connections to Cabinet. They have brothers working in the Prime Minister's office. They themselves may have worked there. Some of them helped the Prime Minister become Prime Minister.
What do you expect Canadians to think, Mr. Speaker, when they see a wheel within a wheel? There is a dark empire, and not registering lobbyists and getting full disclosure encourages and reinforces in the minds of many Canadians, and I tell the Minister this, that something is rotten in the state of Denmark. Every time a contract is let the question would be there at the back of the mind. The only way that can be dealt with, Mr. Minister, is by full disclosure. The system has to be transparent.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Every contract is fully disclosed, as the Hon. Member knows.

We want to know who are the lobbyists approaching civil servants and governments. That is the important part of this legislation. It is extremely important that we should have the information of how much is spent on the lobbying activity for that particular issue that they are lobbying on.
The other thing that we do not like about this Bill is that it sets up a Tier II. That Tier II is for those who are in the employ of a company. For example, INCO has one of its vicepresidents designated as the government relations officer. In other words, he is a consultant. He is a lobbyist on staff. He comes up to the Hill or goes to the bureaucrats to make representations. All he has to declare is his name, address, the name of his company, and its address. He does not have to identify the specific issue.
The same thing applies to associations. The Pharmaceutical Association, for which the former Member for Nickel Belt is now the lobbyist, does not have to declare the particular issue on which it is lobbying. Again, they do not have to disclose the specific issue and the amount of money being spent on that particular issue on which they are lobbying.
The other problem that I have with the Bill, and I speak directly to the Minister, is that it does not register indirect lobbying. In our offices, many of us receive considerable numbers of letters. Most of those letters are worded exactly the same. Who has organized that lobby? Who is spending a considerable amount of bucks in that particular effort? The public wants to know, and we want to know who is behind it. The United States recognized the danger to its open and democratic system, and so it has required registering of indirect lobbying such as I have described.
The other problem with the Bill, which is the one that Frankie baby and the boys at GCI are all on to, and one of the big differences, apart from Gerry Doucet, between GCI and the other consultants, is contingency fees. In other words they have introduced into the waters a white shark. For a fishing
March 8, 1988

licence, 2,000 bucks; access to this Minister, 3,000 bucks; I do this for you, then you pay me. There is a contingency fee now rather than a contract fee. Now the sharks have to be more aggressive. The danger here is that anything goes. To get the fee one has to deliver the contingent. If access to the Minister is not delivered, one does not get paid. Hence one does all sorts of things, like kiss the Minister's toes, his ankles, his knees, and I will stop right there, Mr. Speaker. That is when out comes the lobster, the wine, the champagne, and the painter hats with "Dr. Maz". It leads to and breeds that type of response. They become more aggressive because there is no prohibition against contingency fees in the Bill, none. I see that as a detriment to the Bill, and I would want to correct it.
The other thing that is not in the Bill, and which the standing committee recommended, was that the ADRG-the Assistant Deputy Registrar General-ought to be given some powers to verify information. With respect to verification, this Bill is a toothless rabbit. It has no ability to verify. It has no ability to check out information which has been put on the registry. It has no ability to investigate whether the information that is on the registry is in fact accurate.
It seems to me that this failing in the Bill is detrimental to the Bill. Someone can blow the whistle all he or she wants. Can you see it now, Mr. Speaker, the Member for Gander- Twillingate (Mr. Baker) can blow the whistle, go to the ARDG and say, "I know so and so is not registered and he is lobbying". The ARDG says, "So". I know that the Member would insist that something be done, as any Member would, but the ARDG says, "I have no power to do that. I can't do that". So who, in effect, brings action against the offenders of the Act? Who will do that? Who does that? That is a glaring shortcoming in the Bill. I have some difficulties with that, and I think it should be there.
I do not believe that there should be two tiers in the Bill. As the standing committee recommended, I think that there should be one tier. Everyone who for a fee tries to influence, or makes representation to, should register as a lobbyist. In fact, if I may be so bold as to define lobbyists as stated in my Private Member's Bill which was introduced in the House on February 19, 1987, it is:
"lobbyist" means any person who, for payment, attempts to influence,
directly or indirectly,
(a)	the introduction, passage, defeat or amendment of any legislation before either House of Parliament, or
(b)	a decision to be taken on any matter coming within the administrative jurisdiction of a Minister of the Crown, whether or not that matter has come or is likely to come before either House of Parliament for legislative action;
It seems to me that that is the definition of a lobbyist. One cannot dilute that definition by setting up Tier I and Tier II. In fact, it is very important that in respect of any lobbyist who comes to the Hill and approaches a Member of Parliament, or a member of the bureaucracy, or a staff member, the public has a right to know what is the issue that that person is after.
For example, in the case of INCO, people in the Sudbury basin were interested to know exactly why the vice-president responsible for government relations was approaching their Member of Parliament. What was the issue that the vicepresident was trying to lobby the Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) about? Was it to get a break in the levels of S02 emissions coming out of the stack? Was it from Falconbridge to get a permit to continue shipping out raw nickel to Norway for refining?
I see it is one o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
subsubtopic: RULING AGAINST REGULATION PROHIBITING UNPROCESSED FISH EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) declared that a free trade deal with the United States would create hundreds of thousands of new jobs. When Canadians refused to buy that line, the Prime Minister stated that a free trade deal would protect existing jobs from increasing trade protectionism in the United States.
This is simply not true. Ask the thousands of workers in the British Columbia fishing industry whose jobs are at risk because of the desperate efforts of the federal Government to get a trade deal with the Americans.
Last November the Americans won a decision before the GATT panel against B.C. regulations which prohibit the export of unprocessed fish. Since then the federal Government has done nothing to protect the thousands of jobs that would be lost if the ruling is approved by the full GATT Council. This would have a devastating impact on coastal communities which depend on the fishery.
Last Friday plant workers held work stoppages to protest the federal Government's bungling. This week a delegation of workers is here in Ottawa to express their concerns firsthand.
On behalf of my colleagues in the Liberal Party, I urge the Conservative Cabinet to get its act together and protect those jobs. Anything less is absolutely unacceptable.

March 8, 1988

maintopic: CELEBRATION '88 DEMONSTRATION OF THE OLYMPIC SPIRIT
CELEBRATION '88 DEMONSTRATION OF THE OLYMPIC SPIRIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thanks to the federal Government's Celebration '88 program, all Canadians had a chance to participate in the festivities which were part of the Calgary Olympics.
By virtue of the very hard work of hundreds of volunteers on Celebration '88 award selection committees all across Victoria-Haliburton, 15 communities submitted nominations for awards. It was my distinct pleasure to present medals and certificates at 18 different ceremonies to the most deserving citizens who demonstrated the Olympic spirit in their daily lives.
Even at the Olympic Games in Calgary, I did not see any function at which the pride in our nationhood shone through more brightly than on the faces of thousands of my constituents who came out to support the Olympics through Celebration '88.
On behalf of my constituents and many others who participated in Celebration '88 events, I commend the Government on a job well done.
In the same spirit of pride and accomplishment, I ask all my colleagues, on behalf of Canadians across the country, to welcome appreciatively a number of our finest Olympic athletes when they are introduced to the House in a very few minutes. Let's show them how we feel.

Mr. Speaker, today is a wonderful day of celebration for women around the world. For many decades women have made March 8 their day, that is, International Women's Day, a time to pay respect to the struggles of the past and to seek strength for the work ahead. It is particularly inspiring to remember our foremothers who made today's celebrations possible.
[ Translation]
More especially I have in mind our native sisters who have shown great courage throughout history. Then there are the first immigrant women from Europe and those who are arriving today, quite prepared to begin a new life in Canada,

Women have made very positive contributions to world history. We have struggled for justice, equality, and peace. Today I like to think of Dr. Lise Meitner who, along with a male colleague, was the first to split the atom. A pacifist, she was horrified by the military implications of her discovery and refused to work on the atomic bomb. Not only was she a
pioneer in her own non-traditional field, but she wanted to do things differently.
This is what women are asking for today-equality in a just and peaceful world.

Mr. Speaker, today we are celebrating International Women's Day. Since 1910, March 8 has been a day of renewed involvement for Canadian women. In their homes and communities women are making an unmeasurable contribution to our society.
Mr. Speaker, women account for one half of the talents of the Canadian people. Thanks to the perseverance and determination of women, a number of questions are brought forward and gain political currency. Mr. Speaker, we have the full support of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
The Meech Lake Accord and the free trade initiative again attest to the Government's will to make it easier for women to play an active and leading role in the economic and social life of our country.
Mr. Speaker, today we celebrate our past. Tomorrow we will continue to prepare our future.

Mr. Speaker, this year's Estimates reveal that over-all government spending goes up over 8 per cent, but Environment Canada's budget goes up only 3.5 per cent, less than the rate of inflation. By contrast, the budget of Energy, Mines and Resources is up 30 per cent, Agriculture is up 24 per cent, Fisheries and Oceans is up 23 per cent, Finance is up 13.5 per cent, Indian and Northern Affairs is up 11.5 per cent, Communications is up 11 per cent, National Defence is up 8.3 per cent, and Transport is up 7.3 per cent.
Considering that in poll after poll Canadians say that environmental protection is the most important issue, the 3.5 per cent budget increase of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is pitiful.
Since 1984, Environment Canada's budget has lost $70 million to inflation. Compared to 1984, this year's budget of
March 8, 1988

Environment Canada is weaker by 17 per cent. The contrast between the Minister's rhetoric and his actions is appalling.

subtopic: FIGHT AGAINST RACISM THROUGHOUT THE WORLD
FIGHT AGAINST RACISM THROUGHOUT THE WORLD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Montreal's black community can tell us that racism is not dead in Canada.

The National Congress of Black Women has stated that much must be done by Governments in Canada before the ideal of complete racial equality is achieved. The Congress delivered its message here in the precincts of a Parliament that represents all of the people of Canada equally. Its members were heard with respect, with interest, and with a willingness to pursue change.
What a difference has been dramatized on this International Women's Day between a civilized democracy, such as ours,
and South Africa where white, black, and brown women found that being together merely to talk freedom, equality, and participation is a virtual crime against the state, to be exercised only through subtle strategies lest they place themselves at risk.
They are of the international sisterhood. We share their oppression, and their struggle is ours.

subtopic: NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY-ALLEGED POSITIONS ON BILL C-33
NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY-ALLEGED POSITIONS ON BILL C-33
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two sides to every issue, and Canada's socialist Party often agrees with both.
Last month a brown envelope under my door gave two responses prepared by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) on Bill C-33 for his NDP caucus colleagues.
First, for those who write who are opposed, say the following:
Dear friend, please be assured that I oppose this Bill. I cannot support legislation which will deindex superannuation of federal public servants.
Blah, blah, blah.
Second, for those who write and support this Bill, say the following:
Dear friend, thank you for your letter and your concern for inclusion of benefits in C-33. I and my Party are fully in support of these pension improvements which include survivor benefits, death benefits and equality provisions. We have urged the Government to bring these needed improvements forward as soon as possible.
Blah, blah, blah.
There will be no callouses on the NDP Members from sitting on the fence, just grease for sliding from one side of the issue to the other.

Today being International Women's Day, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize that this year more than ever before, this day should provide us with an opportunity to reflect upon several basic issues which are currently debated in our country.
Whether in the area of abortion, daycare, equal opportunities on the labour market or equal pay for equal work, the Canadian society has more than ever to make choices.
After years of efforts trying to make Canadians aware of the great principles of basic equality between the sexes, we can observe undeniable progress.

March 8, 1988
We must now be twice as careful and make sure that the critical decisions which we will make collectively within the next year will adequately reflect the new realities.

subtopic: FORUM SCHEDULED TO BE HELD ON PARLIAMENT HILL
FORUM SCHEDULED TO BE HELD ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is another step in the long journey for social justice in Canada.
I would like to inform Members of this House that the Parliamentary Committee on Disabled Persons is going to organize a parliamentary forum that will take place here on May 30 on Parliament Hill. This forum will coincide with the first ever National Awareness Week for the Disabled in Canada.
To you personally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say, in light of your strong personal interest and record of accomplishment in this area, what a pleasure it is for me as Chairman of the Committee to be co-hosting that event with you. There will be representation from all provinces and the territorial councils as well as this House.
The forum will be designed to increase awareness of the social and economic issues which affect disabled Canadians, particularly in terms of employment. It will be another example of institutional leadership to show that these matters of concern to all Canadians can be brought forward.
To conclude, I would like to express my personal hope that by the end of 1988 there will exist in provincial Legislatures and Councils committees similar to that which we have here in the House of Commons.

subtopic: ISRAEL-CONDEMNATION OF EXECUTION OF PASSENGERS IN HIJACKED BUS
ISRAEL-CONDEMNATION OF EXECUTION OF PASSENGERS IN HIJACKED BUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last few months, many of us in the House have had occasion to be severely critical of Israel for human rights violations in the occupied territories and for the brutal and often lethal way that Israeli troops have dealt with the Palestinian anger coming at them in the form of stones. Having said that, it now needs to be said that the execution of passengers on a hijacked bus is also morally reprehensible and
certainly is not a milestone on the path to a peace conference, let alone peace.
Whether it was the PLO or a faction of the PLO, whether it was sanctioned by Arafat or designed to undermine him, whether it was designed to disable the peace process or mistakenly thought to be something that would help it along, this hijacking was wrong. I hope I speak for all Members of Parliament when I call on those responsible for this action to think again. A return to terrorism is not the answer.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF LANGUAGE TRAINING FOR IMMIGRANT WOMEN
IMPORTANCE OF LANGUAGE TRAINING FOR IMMIGRANT WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, through today's recognition of International Women's Day it is hoped that all Canadians will celebrate the contributions of women. However, it should also inspire us to be aware of the unique problems which still prevent their fullest participation in and rewards from our Canadian system. Moreover, the difficulties encountered by immigrant visible minority women are vastly multiplied and their failure to obtain adequate language training is at the centre of their nightmares.
If Governments talk about improving the employment, educational and literacy skills of women, then it is absolutely crucial for the federal Government to reform its language training criteria so that immigrant women are not penalized because they happen to be women. We cannot afford to permit them to be ghettoized in their homes and to live isolated from the mainstream of our national life. Like their husbands working outside the home, or their children who attend primary or secondary schools, these women must also have the opportunity to become proficient in either English or French, the first important step toward being a contributing and integrated member of Canadian society. It is therefore urgent that the Government move to make this reality a right rather than a privilege.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are proud of them all.
My question is directed to the Minister responsible for the status of women. She knows that the industries facing the greatest threat under the proposed Canada-U.S. trade agreement will be the manufacturing and service industries. The Minister also knows that women make up 63 per cent of the labour force in manufacturing industries, indeed 78 per cent in the clothing industry alone, and 80 per cent of the labour force in the service industries.
Will the Minister tell us what action the Government intends to take to ensure that the jobs of these women are not jeopardized by the trade deal, and what new assistance the Government will propose in order to provide adjustment and assistance for the women whose jobs are being thrown at risk?

speechtext:

Yesterday the Minister revealed that he is unaware that the GATT ruling against the B.C. fishing industry is contrary to the Law of the Sea, is contrary to the Canada-U.S. Salmon Treaty, and is a fishing issue, not a trade issue.
Since the Government understood the sovereign right to protect processing and conservation and protected the fishing industries in Quebec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland from U.S. interference, why is the Government planning to support a proposal tomorrow in Washington which will gut the B.C. industry and place the entire Atlantic fishing industry at risk?

I made clear yesterday that there have been extensive negotiations and discussions with the industry and with the provinces, and that Canada went to the other nations involved in the GATT panel and made our case. We did not succeed in that case, so we are now meeting again, tomorrow, to see if there are other ways in which we could proceed to resolve this very serious question.
Of course the other matter that arises is that the New Democratic Party on GATT issues speaks out of both sides of its mouth. It supports GATT in principle, it claims, yet in practice it wants us to get out of the GATT.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same Minister and is on the point of consistency.
We have a $750 million industry in British Columbia, principally employing women in high-paying, unionized jobs. They are not ghettoized as they are in many areas of the Canadian economy. There are 7,500 jobs at risk.
When the Americans find GATT rulings that they do not like on Canadian oil, on Spanish soybeans, and on trade
embargoes with Nicaragua, they do not implement them. The Minister of Fisheries says that he opposes the GATT ruling, but he has been muzzled by Cabinet.
I want to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he is going to stand up and show consistency. You protected the five Atlantic provinces. You forgot about British Columbia. What is going on? Why not protect the workers of B.C.?

The New Democratic Party is talking out of both sides of its mouth, and it should stop doing that in the interest of consistency and in the interest of honesty.

speechtext:

Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberger) raised an issue relating to announcements made by the Ministry of Fisheries and Oceans regarding Chinook salmon, including a major announcement of new enhancement on the Cowichan River which is in my constituency. speechtext: When the House rose at 1 o'clock p.m. the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying before the lunch hour interrupted me, and if my memory trusts me well, we have no problem with the principle of Bill C-82. We support the principle, but there are issues in the Bill, things that we would like to see tightened up. In brief, we mention the provision of a two tier system. There is no need for a two tier system of registry of lobbyists. We ought to have one tier of registry of lobbyists.
Second, the Bill does not provide for a prohibition of contingency lobbying. We believe that this is a shortcoming in the Bill. The fact is that attaching a fee by a lobbyist for the accomplishment of the lobbying objectives is, in our view, contrary to the kinds of presentations which lobbyists make to bureaucrats and to Members of Parliament.
Third, we believe that the Bill ought to have prohibited the indirect lobbying by mass mailings which, in our discovery in the jurisdiction of the United States, are covered by U.S. lobbying legislation. In fact, that could be one method used to circumvent the intent of this Bill.
There is no doubt in my mind, and recent surveys reflect this, that Canadians have lost confidence in the ability of their political leaders when it comes to honesty, ethics and a whole host of other issues that are very important to the democratic process. I think that is what the Prime Minister sensed when, in 1985, in a letter to Members of Parliament, he recognized
Lobbyists Registration Act
that lobbyists had to be registered. Subsequently, events have shown that there are questionable activities by lobbyists at this time, activities that can only serve to reinforce in the minds of Canadians the notion that politicians deal with ethical matters and matters of state in questionable ways.
I said earlier today that registering lobbyists is the completion of a process of open Government. We have the freedom of information legislation and the election expenses legislation. These pieces of legislation were all implemented to create a greater transparency in Government, to provide Canadians with more information about the manner in which they are governed. If contributions are made to Parties or to individuals, they are on the record. The public has access to that information. That can only serve to buttress democracy in a system such as ours. This piece of legislation which provides for the registering of lobbyists is indeed extremely important to the process.
It is unfortunate that the Bill is lacking in what I would call teeth. There is no provision in the Bill for the Assistant Deputy Registrar General to verify the information which lobbyists will put in the registry. There is no way of initiating any investigation-
