speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Elon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, one of the shortcomings of the Bill is that it gives the Assistant Deputy Registrar General no power to verify the information which lobbyists will put on the registry. The ADRG has no power to conduct investigations. The Bill does not even say who can initiate an action.
If a Member of Parliament or a civil servant brings to the attention of the ADRG a lobbyist who is not acting within the parameters of the Bill, who initiates the action? Who verifies it, who collects the information, who starts the process? Nothing in the Bill ascribes that particular function to the ADRG.
We think the Bill must be improved. While we agree with the Bill in principle, we believe that in committee we will use every opportunity to amend the Bill in order to strengthen it. We hope that the Government will see that our amendments are useful and helpful and will provide the kind of transparency and openness which I believe Canadians demand and would welcome.
I must point out that the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure, on which I served, studied the question of a lobbying registry and visited the closest jurisdiction which has a registry of lobbyists. Within the group, there were those who really did not feel the need for such registration. When we went to the United States to look into this matter. There were those who were convinced that there was no need for a registry of lobbyists and that in fact we ought to leave the lobbyists to regulate themselves.
When we met with lobbyists in the United States, one of the questions we put to them was what would be the main thrust of their proposals if they were in our spot and had to draft registry rules for lobbyists. They all said, almost with one voice, that they would make it tough. This blew the minds of the Conservative members of the committee who were not wedded to that idea. They were absolutely shocked that lobbyists would demand that lobbying legislation be tough.
When the lobbyists explained the reasons for saying that, we found that their argument was quite reasonable. They said they wanted to ensure that a code be established for them within the legal framework because that is how they convince clients that they operate under a very strict legal code and under the laws of the country. That is the best guarantee that the client will be getting professional services.
The lobbyists to whom we spoke were proud to run off computer lists of their clients and their charges to show to the committee. It was interesting to note that well-known multinationals and other corporations were on that list as well as the issues they were lobbying for and the amounts of money
charged. That is what we will be promoting in our amendments when we get to committee. We will be looking for that kind of openness in the legislation.
It seems to me that people who want to do business with the Government ought to be doing so, but Canadians ought to be able to know who they are and what they are charging. That is a system that is accountable as well as transparent.
The other question with which we dealt as a committee was foreign lobbyists from foreign Governments. In our report we recognized that foreign Governments have embassies here in Ottawa and they have government-to-government relations. They consult with Departments, and we have excluded them from our recommendations on lobbying. I notice that they are not included in the Bill.
In conclusion, I want to say that Bill C-82 is a small step, but it is a step in the right direction. We have to move this Bill forward as quickly as possible into committee. I support the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell	(Mr. Boudria) who made a wise suggestion. While we originally recommended that the Bill should be sent to the committee that studied the lobbying question, he said it should go to a legislative committee, hopefully made up of members of the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure, for study. I hope the Government will follow that suggestion.
We hope the Minister has listened attentively to the points we have raised and recognizes that we are not trying to destroy the Bill. We want to make it better, more effective, and make Government more open and accountable. Therefore we hope the suggestions we have made will find their way into the Bill as amendments.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words on this Bill. I think some of the suggestions made by the Hon. Member who just spoke should be taken into account by the Minister when this Bill gets to committee stage. Some of the points raised are very important. Perhaps I can just review those points.
Keep in mind that since 1984 we have seen a great proliferation of lobbying firms throughout the country. They are engaged in various activities for the benefit of certain clients; not that there is anything wrong with that. Yet some of those clients who received favourable attention from the Government might have gotten it anyway without hiring the lobbying firm. In fact, I would say in a great many cases it is a tremendous waste of money to hire one of these lobbying outfits when the client could perhaps see hers or his own local Member of Parliament or make representations directly to the Government.
The Bill defines professional lobbyists as:
Every individual who, for payment, on behalf of any person or organization-undertakes to arrange a meeting with a public office holder or to communicate with a public office holder in an attempt to influence
March 8, 1988

(a)	the development of a legislative proposal by the Government of
Canada-
That means someone who was hired to arrange for the presentation of a Bill before the Elouse of Commons. It then goes on to say someone who attempts to influence:
(b)	the introduction, passage, defeat or amendment of any Bill-
In other words, any individual, organization or group interested in amending a Bill.
Then it says:
(c)	the making of any regulation, order or other instrument-
Which, as you know, are made by the Government of Canada. Then it talks about the development of any policy by the Government. That is a general enough clause in the Bill which would probably cover anything having to do with public policy.
Then it talks about the appointment of individuals to any body or office. I suppose, for example, if someone wanted to be appointed to the Senate or some board and hired a lobbying firm to do that, they would be covered by that part. Then it refers to the awarding of any grant, contribution or similar benefit, or a contract by the Government.
What must that person or group do? They must register with the registrar not later than 10 days after entering into the undertaking. If they do not, what happens? Under the offences part it says:
Every individual who contravenes or fails to comply with any provision of
this Act is guilty of an offence-
What will happen to them if they are brought before a court? There is a fine of not more than $25,000 or a trip to prison for a term not to exceed six months. Then it says in Clause 13(b):
-on proceedings by way of indictment, to a fine not exceeding one hundred
thousand dollars and to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years-
In other words, the value of someone's time outside of a prison is seen by this Act to be about $50,000 a year. If you can pay $50,000 you do not have to go to jail for a year. If you cannot pay it, then off you go. It is very interesting to look at some of these Acts and see how much time adds up to $1,000 in the view of our legal system. It means if you have lots of money, you do not have to serve any of these jail terms.
I suppose the Bill sounds pretty conclusive. It is fairly thorough. There is a problem, though, as some speakers have pointed out. You do not really have to register if you call yourself a public relations firm, I suppose. You do not have to say how much money you are getting for your lobbying activities. There are several lobbying firms here in Ottawa and in provincial capitals, and under this Act they are not going to have to say how much money they receive, whether it is $1,000 or $100,000 or $1 million. They should have to. What was the value of their input to the Government of Canada?
I would like to suggest to the Minister another area which is perhaps not covered at all under this legislation but which
Lobbyists Registration Act
should be. Perhaps he can address this in committee or at third reading. The problem is this. If you examine all of the sales by agencies of the federal Government this year and last you will see something interesting, for example, the sale of the hotels owned by Canadian National just recently. What was the procedure used? The bids on those hotels had to be received by someone from someone. In other words, there were people in Canada interested in bidding on the Chateau Laurier and the Hotel Newfoundland and every other CN hotel right across Canada. Someone had to receive those bids. The Cabinet approved the sale, as was brought out in Question Period today.
Who determined which was the best bid or who would get those hotels for that particular amount of money? It said in the bidding process that not necessarily the highest bid would be accepted. It got into the hands of the Cabinet because the people involved who wanted to buy those hotels had hired lobbying firms. Canadian National hired a consulting firm in New York to arrange the bids, to seek out the prospective bidders and then prepare a document for the board of Canadian National, who looked at the recommendation of the consulting firm from New York and either accepted or rejected it. It then sent its recommendation to the federal Cabinet for approval or rejection.
The lobbying firms that were hired by those bidders did not lobby a government official, a cabinet Minister or any of the people named in this Bill.
Some of the lobbying firms that were mentioned in the House today by the two Members who spoke previously are being hired today to lobby on behalf of certain interests to buy two telephone companies in Canada. Northwest Tel, which covers all the Northwest Territories, is up for sale by the Government of Canada. That telephone company is very profitable. It made between $8 million and $10 million in net profits last year and pumped millions of dollars in capital expenditures. One could likely get a profit of $20 million from Northwest Tel.
Another telephone company in the eastern part of Canada, Terra Nova Telecommunications, is also owned by the federal Government. It made a profit of approximately $5 million and pumped $11 million into its capital expansion. Some of the consulting firms named in the House today have been hired by interests who want to purchase those profitable telephone companies. Telephone companies are licensed to make money because their profits are guaranteed.
The consumers must pay and the telephone companies will make the profits. We even have public bodies that are appointed to ensure these companies make a reasonable profit, one that is not too much or too little.
In this situation a consulting firm is hired in Ottawa to lobby on behalf of another telephone company that wishes to purchase Terra Nova Telecommunications and a telephone

March 8, 1988
Lobbyists Registration Act
company on the West Coast that wishes to purchase Northwest Telephone. These consulting firms are being paid enormous amounts of money through their offices in Ottawa, Vancouver, Toronto and St. John's, Newfoundland, to work on these proposals on behalf of big business interests in Canada.
These lobbying firms are of quite some prominence in Canada. Indeed, I noticed that one of the lobbying firms is headed by a former prominent Conservative Member of Parliament from Newfoundland. He was hired by a telephone company in Newfoundland to prepare a bid for the purchase of Terra Nova Telecommunications.
One must question whether these consulting firms, which are being paid substantial amounts of money, are covered under this Bill. I am willing to bet that the successful bidder on the stock exchange for Terra Nova Telecommunications will be Newfoundland Telephone. I believe it will be successful because not only can it offer a large amount of money, it certainly has a foot in the door. I suggest that even the other bidders who will be putting forward their bids for the purchase of that extremely profitable telephone company realize that fact.
The same thing is happening with Northwest Telephone in northern Canada. Consulting firms are being hired at varying costs. Certainly, the lobbying firms are making a bundle of money.
My objection is that I do not believe these procedures are covered under this legislation. In other words, the lobbying firm hired by Newfoundland Telephone in Newfoundland should have to register under this legislation and indicate that it is hired for the express purpose of trying to get a successful bid for the purchase of Terra Nova Telecommunications. There should then be a requirement on the part of the lobbying firms hired by telephone companies in western Canada for the purchase of Northwest Telephone.
The current arrangement is that an accounting firm has been designated by Canadian National to handle the sale of Northwest Telephone. In the case of Terra Nova Telecommunications, the bids are submitted to the consulting firm of Canada Capital Corporation, which I understand is a very competent company in downtown Toronto. It does all the research, prepares the bids, and accepts them on behalf of Canadian National. The bids then go to the board of Canadian National who make their judgment and send that to the federal Cabinet for its decision.
I would like the Minister to address this complicated procedure when he addresses the Bill either in committee stage or at third reading.
If the lobbying firms are to assume control over what happens, when, where and how in all of these decisions in Canada, we should certainly know the identity of these lobbying firms and how much they are being paid. They should not be allowed to hide behind a consulting firm from New York State, as in the case of Canadian National hotels where
the bid can go back to the board of CN and then to Cabinet for final approval. Who is trying to fool whom?
We now have the case of the telephone companies and the lobbying firms. I know personally the lobbyists who have been hired. They know the system intimately. They know what to do, and when, to make sure their clients meet with success.
I do hope the Minister will take that into account because that is one of the big loopholes. The other, as I mentioned, is the salary. For goodness' sake, we should know how much these fellows are raking in when they are successful in purchasing a telephone company for $180 million, or $200 million in the case of Northwest Telephone. How much are the consulting firms being paid? Is it 5 per cent? Is it 10 per cent? We are into big money here and we should know how much they are being paid. We all know who they are, but I would love to know how much these fellows are being paid for performing the job.
I have one word of caution, however, for these companies. I think in a lot of cases it is a waste of money. I think probably if the right bid was submitted, if it was the highest bid, they should not have to worry. There should be some procedure whereby they can appeal, certainly to the federal Cabinet, if they are not treated fairly. Perhaps they are wasting their money by going to these lobbying firms.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, I have made a prediction that a particular company will be successful in its bid to purchase Terra Nova Telecommunications very shortly. I have made the prediction and it is on the official record. Watch for it, Mr. Speaker, because that is what is going to happen.

Mr. Speaker, I am looking at this lobbyist legislation and I would like to make some comments and ask a question. In the interpretation, "public office holder" is defined as a member of the Senate or the House of Commons and an individual who is appointed by the Governor in Council, an officer, director or employee of any federal board, a member of the Canadian Armed Forces and a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I wonder if the mandarins were forgotten. I mean the upper echelon bureaucrats, the deputy ministers, the assistant deputy ministers and the program officers. The lobbyist tries to influence in order to get a contract and, naturally, at one point he is going to see the deputy minister, the assistant deputy minister or the person who develops the program. I wonder if they should not be included in this Bill. Could the Hon. Member give me an opinion on whether he believes that the mandarins, who really run this country, the permanent Government of Canada, should be included in the Bill? I do not see why a member of the RCMP should be included. He does not give any favours. But why are the mandarins not in the definition of "public office holder"?

Mr. Speaker, looking at the section to which the Hon. Member is referring I would have to say right off the bat
March 8, 1988

that I agree that certainly they should be included. However, under the interpretation section, Clause 2(1), it states that "public office holder" means any officer or employee of Her Majesty in right of Canada and includes a member of the Senate or the House of Commons, an individual appointed to any office or body with the approval of the Governor in Council, which is the Cabinet, or a Minister of the Crown, an officer, or director of any federal board or commission, a member of the Canadian Armed Forces and a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Perhaps the Hon. Member could inform me as to whether he believes that that clause excludes certain public servants. The normal way of drafting that definition, 1 believe, would be the way it is done. In other words, it says "public office holder' means any officer or employee of Her Majesty in right of Canada, and it includes a specific list under the general definition. As a former Law Clerk of a legislature, I would say that this would cover all the public servants to which the hon. gentleman referred, but perhaps he has additional information or an interpretation from the drafter of the legislation that is to the contrary.

I appreciate the comments of the Hon. Member. Naturally, as he indicates, these persons are defined under "public office holder". I wonder whether it would be better to have another section saying that this includes as well all civil servants in the employ of a Minister, so it would be more specific and precise and not left to the interpretation of a judge or the bureaucrats.

Perhaps, for clarity, you will notice, Mr. Speaker, in certain definitions when it makes a broad statement as to interpretation and definition, the hon. gentleman is partially correct, because sometimes it gives the general meaning, and in this particular case it means any officer or employee of Her Majesty in right of Canada, which means everyone that the federal Government pays. Then, as the hon. gentleman points out, there could be a period there and it could say: "This definition includes", and it could list whatever should be listed, but then it could be repeated in the first section what is said in the preamble. It could be reiterated in that way.
I would suggest that the Hon. Member make that point to the Minister as a matter of clarity. We have some of the finest drafters of legislation in the world employed by the federal Government in the Department of Justice. We have the same quality of drafters in the provincial administration. They are some of the finest in the world. A great many of them have come over from Scotland and Great Britain and they are very fine drafters of legislation. The problem is not with the drafters of the legislation. The problem is with the Government because it gives them things which cannot really be drafted properly by anyone.

Mr. Speaker, I just have a couple of brief points. First, on the question of the definition of "public office holder", it is quite clear in my mind that this covers everyone
Lobbyists Registration Act
who is an employee of the federal Government. The reason the committee in its report recommended that everyone be covered lies in the fact that in the United States of America the law states that lobbying activity only occurs when a lobbyist meets an elected person. That, of course, is not good enough. We wanted to include everyone. In my opinion, the Minister has done that. If it can be further clarified, that is all right with me, as long as it covers everyone.
I want to direct a question on a slightly different topic to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker). I want to congratulate him, by the way, for his excellent speech. I am sure you would want me to do that, Mr. Speaker. I am of the opinion that the Bill should include a provision to disallow such a thing as contingency fees. I think it is an acceptable practice in the legal profession, at least in some provinces, that one cannot charge a contingency fee. In other words one cannot say, "Mr. So-and-so, I will get you an appointment with the Minister to get you a fishing licence, and that will cost you $2,000. However, if you are successful in your application you owe me another $8,000". In the unlikely event that a lobbyist would want to do something like that, I think it should be disallowed, not that any lobbyist would ever want to do anything like that.
I want to ask my colleague whether or not he agrees that that type of a contingency fee would or should be unacceptable since it is not accepted in the legal profession, at least in most provinces. As a matter of fact, it would be disallowed in most of the states of the United States.

Mr. Speaker, of course the point is that we will never know if there is a contingency fee or if there is a sliding fee, a flat fee, an advance fee, an after-thought fee, or any other kind of fee. We will never know because under the legislation nothing has to be declared. The Hon. Member's point is very well taken.
What has happened in a great many of these cases today in which lobbying firms represent companies to try to get something out of the Government is that some of these firms have formed other lobbying firms and the same people might be lobbying both sides of the same issue. In that case there is an almost assured contingency fee no matter who gets it. What has happened is that they have become quite prominent in Canada. All of the big bidders, such as the telephone companies which are now bidding for these two particular telephone companies which are up for sale in Canada, Northwest Tel and Terra Nova Telecommunications, are putting up big bids. Bids of some $150 million and $200,000 are coming in today. Those great telephone companies have guaranteed profits. I believe they have all hired the same firms, which are all interconnected in the bidding.
If we were to boil it down we should at least know who these companies are. There should be a referee somewhere. One of them has to have the successful bid. But it should be advertised

as to how much profit is being made out of it as well as how much money they are charging. Some of these lobbyists are becoming multimillionaires.

speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 66, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Andre that Bill C-82, an Act respecting the registration of lobbyists, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, to put it mildly the Bill we are discussing today is long overdue. It was on September 9, 1985, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in an open letter to all Members of Parliament and Senators stated:
It is a great principle of public administration-I could even say an 'imperative'-that to function effectively the government and the public service of a democracy must have the trust and confidence of the public they serve. In order to reinforce that trust, the government must be able to provide constant management and, above all, to be guided by the highest standards of conduct.
He then went on to outline a number of measures he proposed to bring forward to achieve the aims which he outlined in the paragraph from which I have just quoted, including a new conflict of interest post-employment code for public office holders; instructions to Ministers imposing specific and strict limitations on the hiring of family members; and letters to the Leaders of the Opposition on the subject of ethical standards for MPs and Senators. Later on in the same letter he referred to the conflict of interest code and said:
Among my first actions upon assuming office was to give the Deputy Prime Minister a mandate to: review existing conflict of interest and postemployment guidelines-
The fifth item on this list was with respect to lobbying legislation. He stated:
The fifth component of this comprehensive approach to public sector ethics is the undertaking of this Government to introduce into the House of Commons, at an early date, legislation to monitor lobbying activity and to control the lobbying process by providing a reliable and accurate source of information on the activities of lobbyists.
If two and a half years from the time that that letter was written is an early date, then I would hate to think of what a late date would be.
This Bill is not just one to register lobbyists but a response to the very serious problems concerning the activities of many people in public life and their subsequent or related activities. Perhaps the most singular thing about this thirty-third Parliament is that the beginning of 1984 marked the first opportunity for a major change in patronage appointments since 1963.
Those of us who watched the debate held between the leaders of the three political Parties just before the election of 1984 saw the present Prime Minister say to the former Prime Minister, now the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), that he had an option. When he agreed to appoint to the Senate and to other positions Liberals recommended by former Prime Minister Trudeau the Prime Minister said at the time that the Leader of the Official Opposition had an option. He said that he did not have to make those appointments.
The present Prime Minister had an option. He could have brought this legislation and other legislation forward a long time ago. But he did not.
There are two pictures of this Prime Minister. The first version is of him as the Leader of the Opposition going around to Conservative Party meetings entertaining those gatherings by listing the patronage appointments made by the Liberal Governments and saying that the Government he headed would appoint Senators, judges, and we would probably have to wait about a hundred years until anybody but a Conservative received an appointment. Then there was the version that I spoke about a few minutes ago when he said to the present Leader of the Official Opposition that he had an option, he could have done things differently.
This Prime Minister has continued and probably accelerated the rate at which he and his Government have made patronage appointments. He and his Government have handed out patronage appointments and contracts to people without very much concern about whether they are the best, the cheapest or anything else.
I would now like to say something about the comments made by my friend from Newfoundland who spoke before I did. Those of us who are here who were here during the Liberal years remember how Liberal Governments awarded contracts for the building of huge office buildings to various
March 8, 1988

people, including Mr. Teron and Mr. Campeau, without calling for bids. They did extremely well. The Government is now rewarding its friends and some of its former friends with the type of ability given to the new public relations organizations, the new lobby organizations which have grown so quickly under this Conservative Government.
Some of those operators have to be given credit because they have been wise enough not to restrict the membership and the benefits of lobbying organizations only to Conservatives. We see the establishment of the organization headed by a former Conservative Member of Parliament from Newfoundland, later the Premier of Newfoundland, who established Government Consultants International. This organization includes not only Mr. Moores, but Gerry Doucet, former Liberal cabinet Minister, Francis Fox, and others. They have grown. One has to ask, what do they do that permits them to be so successful? How is it that they are able to get the type of clients that they have in such a short period of time?
I wish to put on the record some of their clients. Mercedes-Benz; Saint John Shipbuilding Ltd., which was awarded a $3.5 billion contract to build the six navy frigates; Iron Ore Co. of Canada, which was headed by the present Prime Minister before he entered Parliament; American Express Canada; Nabisco Brands Canada. The President of this company in the United States, Ross Johnson, is a Manitoba native who is a very close friend of the Prime Minister. We are here today to talk about the infamous Bill C-82. It is an Act respecting the registration of lobbyists. We have to hearken back for a moment and remember on what infamous day was this particular piece of legislation first spoken about in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, on September 9, 1985, the Prime Minister published an open letter to all Members and all Senators.

You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that in September, 1985 the Prime Minister came into the House with his new ethics package. He introduced an open letter to all Members and Senators in which he outlined his attack and how he was going to clean up the ethics in government. We had a very hefty document. It was actually englobed in a blue ribbon. In a very proud way the Prime Minister stood up in the House and said "Mr. Speaker, these are the toughest conflict of interest guidelines in the western world. Coupled with those guidelines,
I am going to be moving on a law to seek the registration of lobbyists. That was in 1985 before the situation with the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), and before the litany of scandals which have plagued this Government and after the Prime Minister said that he had already introduced the toughest guidelines in the western world.
What can we draw from that, Mr. Speaker? You can have the toughest criminal code in the world, but it does not stop people from robbing banks. If people want to rob banks or if they want to be dishonest either in government or in the application of their government contacts, they will do so and it will be so. There is no way that any law, however well meaning, can actually legislate the ethical standards of people who are in political life and people who seek to serve the political process in the form of lobbying.
Let us not be bound by the mistaken impression that a Bill, whether it be Bill C-82 or the new conflict of interest guidelines or the old conflict of interest guidelines, which were supposedly the toughest in the western world, can solve the problem. The guidelines are the laws that will lay out the law of the land, but if people want to get around that law they will find ways of doing so. It is our job by way of this particular legislation to make it as difficult as possible for anybody who intends to subvert or to break the intent of the registration of lobbyists. I am not optimistic that the mere introduction of an Act, which we have not yet seen come to fruition-I am glad the Government has finally brought it forward-will solve the problem of lobbyists. In 1985 the Prime Minister said he was going to bring a Bill forward in this regard at the earliest possible opportunity, that speed was of the essence. Here we are in 1988 and we are only now debating the second reading of the said subject.
Let us look at examples where we do have fairly strict regulations governing the registration of lobbyists, namely, in the United States. In the United States, those who represent foreign Governments or lobbying interests are required to register as either a foreign or a paid domestic lobbyist. The current system in the United States consists of political action committees funded in very large measure by either large corporations or large unions which want to promote specific philosophies or policies. No one would want to see the type of political indebtedness that we see in the United States come to Canada. Unfortunately, the new development in lobbying is that Canadian politicians are becoming more and more subject to the artful measures taken by paid lobbyists to get their companies through to a Minister. That is an attempt to subvert the democratic process. It is not an attempt just to provide information but in fact it is an attempt to get a contract through a bureaucrat or a Minister.
An article most recently published in The Globe and Mail's Report on Business by Stevie Cameron entitled "Like Magic" outlines the new direction Canadian lobbying firms are taking. It is a new direction which does not bode well for the democratic and political process in Canada. The author takes some time to examine in the article the work of Government Consultants International and writes:

Fishermen who wanted to put forward their perspective on an issue with a particular Minister tried and tried through the normal democratic process to get through, but it was not until a phone call came from Mr. Moores that finally action came forward. That says to me that lobbying firms in Canada are going in a new direction.
Instead of telling their clients that since they live in a democracy, they have the same right as every other Canadian to have access to their politicians and Ministers, and instead of advising their clients on how best to get through to their Ministers by contacting local Members of Parliament in their constituencies, by coming to Ottawa and by meeting with bureaucrats, lobbyists are being paid to make the contacts. They use their clubby former political contacts with Ministers to open doors that are not open to the average citizen of Canada.
Frankly, the legislation that is being proposed will do nothing to subvert that very dangerous trend in lobbying. Unfortunately, lobbying in Canada is moving in the direction of the establishment of the political action committees which have been established in the United States. Any of us who have studied the American system will know that once a politician is hostage to a political action committee, he or she no longer has the right to speak out on issues about which he or she feels very strongly because he or she will have to check first with the PAC. Political Parties or individual politicians cannot take independent stands because someone in the background is footing the bills. Unfortunately, we are seeing that kind of thing with lobbying in Canada.
This particular Bill does not deal with the issue of contingency fees. It does not deal with who makes the contacts and who is being contacted. It is fine to tell GCI to register. Of course GCI will register like every other lobby firm will, and the Tier I firms will register in one way and Tier II firms will register in another way. Unless we have access to more information about the very special relationship that is established between a Minister and an employee of GCI, for example, there is no way that the public can have confidence that GCI is not simply selling its political connections to secure contracts and financial and monetary benefits for its clients.
One of the ways to solve that problem would be full disclosure. We might broaden this legislation to provide not only that companies register but that they provide quarterly statements which include their client base, fees paid, and a chronology of when a Minister or the Government is contacted for the purpose of lobbying. fishermen's union cannot get through to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) but a phone call from Frank Moores will rectify that, there is no way we can stop that kind of abuse. We must call for fuller disclosure.

It is a move that has been made necessary as a result of a series of questions that have been raised about the activities of the Government and the way it does business. De facto we need to have the registration of lobbyists. However, the registration of lobbyists in and of itself will not solve the problem, which is that we are travelling down a very slippery slope. The ultimate result of that will be a country that is controlled not by Parliament, not by members of all three political Parties who reach a consensus or at least have an honest and open vote in the House of Commons on the issues, but by people behind the scenes who can pay to have access to Ministers in a way that no ordinary Canadian could ever expect.
We have to be realistic about this. We know that both formally and informally, constituents, businesses, unions and voluntary organizations all seek to improve their own communications with Government. Far be it from us to say that there is no role to be played by lobbying firms. There is a role. It is to educate the customer, the consumer and the constituent as to how he or she may best get his or her particular viewpoint expressed in Parliament.
The lobbyist's role is to say, for example, to the Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario or the Canadian Nurses' Association that if it wants to effect change, if it wants to see its profession represented nationally in a way that it is not currently represented, these are the steps that should be followed. It only makes common sense to make these tools available to voluntary organizations as well as paid businesses. However, there is a quantum leap between that kind of initiative and the kind which provides that if a company wants to get a contract, it has to go to Frank Moores because Frank Moores can deliver the Government's dollars. That is not lobbying, that is trading on a political connection which is not available to the public.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in this debate on the motion of the Liberal Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). I would like to state at the outset, and emphasize, as has been done in previous debates on this very motion, the importance the Government places on the issue of ozone depletion. I want Hon. Members to know that this has been exemplified in the role Canada has played in the development of the Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer. Canada was the first nation to ratify this in June of 1986 and continues to play a role in the implementation of the Montreal protocol on substances that deplete the ozone layer, which Canada signed with 23 other nations and the European Economic Community in September of last year. Canada, hopefully, will be among the first nations to ratify, under authority of the new Canadian Environmental Protection Act currently before a legislative committee.
What is really important is that the Government and this House did not really require the Hon. Member to bring forward such a resolution because of the actions initiated by the Government, actions which are light years ahead of the previous administration in recognizing and dealing with a problem of grave importance to all countries. We recognize that the ozone layer is a shared responsibility. Governments, industries, environmental groups and consumer groups all have important roles to play in addressing this serious problem and in our endeavour to correct it.
For example, consumers can play an important role by expressing their preference for products which do not destroy the ozone layer. I believe everyone in the House will recognize that if these products are identified in such a way it will be a beginning. This was clearly demonstrated through consumer groups' involvement in the Government's announcement to ban CFCs and certain aerosol products back in the mid 1970s.
Industry also has accepted its role in the development of environmentally safe products and technologies. At a conference on substitutes and alternatives to CFCs and halons in Washington in January of this year, which Environment Canada co-sponsored with the United States Environmental Protection Agency and the Conservation Foundation, over 700 representatives of industry, environmental groups and Governments from over 20 countries expressed a consensus viewpoint that action is needed now.
Industry described new programs and initiatives to reduce emissions and to find environmentally acceptable substitutes for CFCs and halons. For example, the major producers of these chemicals announced a joint toxicity program costing some $8 million to facilitate information transfer and thereby speed up the process of bringing environmentally acceptable substitutes to the market. I think this also demonstrates that through the actions of this Government and through the actions of private industry, the assimilation of knowledge by
March 8, 1988

everyone interested in doing something about this problem has increased significantly.
What about Government itself? The Hon. Member stated in his motion that Government should consider the advisability of intensifying research for alternatives to CFCs and refrigerants. Certainly, research is fundamental to getting environmentally safe substitutes to market. But given the potential profits, is this not an activity that would be best left to the private sector? For its part, the international community has created a glowing market opportunity for envirnomentally acceptable substitute chemicals and products by setting consumption reduction targets in the Montreal protocol, and industry has responded by beefing up its research into alternatives.
What is significant about those activities is that the private sector has taken up the challenge. It has in fact very quickly moved because it can see this as being profitable to itself. As consumers have a better understanding of some of the harmful uses of certain chemicals, they would preferably want to purchase something that would not harm the environment.
I would submit that Government can be much more effective in dealing with ozone layer depletion by putting in place a control strategy which will decrease industrial and consumer demand and hence decrease consumption of ozone depleting chemicals. The Government in fact has begun to put together the elements of such a strategy. I would like to describe this briefly in general terms to give an idea of the general direction we are presently considering. Before I do that, let me emphasize once again that Canada is fully committed to ratifying the Montreal protocol and to meeting the reductions set out therein. The Government has had a lot of meaningful discussions in this particular area and it is abundantly clear that we are about to move on this in a very forthright manner.
In order to develop the necessary regulatory controls to accomplish this, we will need the legislative authorities contained in the new Canadian Environmental Protection Act which is currently before a parliamentary committee. I had the privilege of sitting on that committee and listening to the Hon. Member who proposed the motion argue and debate the good and bad points of changing the Bill or making it stronger. I think his interjection is welcomed. It is fair and it is useful, although it is a little out of time now to be debating such a motion. However, the Hon. Member has taken a keen interest in the subject. And I am sure he will continue to do so in that interest.
In order to carry out this analysis, we must gather information from industry concerning the amounts of CFCs and halons produced, consumed and traded. We must also consider the impact on industry and the numbers of jobs that may be affected by any regulatory decision we may take. Members of the oppositions Parties from time to time criticize the Government because an industry may have lay-offs. Let us be honest enough to say that actions taken by this Government and other Governments and businesses in this field around the world may

affect someone's job. I think the Government has realized that and has in fact set forth areas of assistance. In return for a greater environmental control of our globe, we are prepared to accept the fact that some jobs may be jeopardized and, if so, I am sure this Government will take the appropriate action to compensate those affected or retrain them.
These activities are well under way and we intend to have a control options report available later this summer or early this fall. This report will be the starting point for our multistakeholder consultative process. We will be seeking the views of all concerned parties on the pros and cons of these options.
This is a tremendous step forward for the Government on the environment. I think it is appropriate from time to time for the opposition critics to ask the Government what it is doing. I think, though, in this short 10 minutes, I have been able to demonstrate that we have done a tremendous amount. We are not shirking our responsibility. We are taking the environment, the ozone layer, as a very serious matter. We will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, 1 begin by saying that I do not know what the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) said when he first spoke to this Bill. However, I think that the Hon. Member for Selkirk- Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) should see Private Members' Business for what it is. If you like, Mr. Speaker, the tone of the Hon. Member's remarks was inappropriate to what this hour is about.
He mentioned the Montreal protocol. Certainly we were all glad of the Montreal protocol. Although, according to the judgment of those who are concerned about the ozone layer, it fell short of what we would have liked to see. However, at the time, and still, one has to remark that it was a significant achievement, not just with respect to the ozone layer but with respect to the fact of having an international protocol at all. There are many other matters with respect to which we would love to have an international protocol, whether it be on acid rain or a variety of other environmental problems. We do not have them. So in so far as the Montreal protocol, given its limits, sets a precedent, we hope that it will be precedentsetting and that we will see other global protocols with respect to global environmental problems.
The Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake derided the notion that the Government should be involved in the intensification of research with respect to finding substitutes for freon and other substances that release the chlorofluorocarbons that eventually erode the ozone layer. I do not think that it is an inappropriate suggestion on the part of the Hon. Member for Davenport at all. I think that what the Hon. Member for

March 8, 1988

Selkirk-Interlake does not realize is the urgency with which this problem should be viewed.
We have an eroding ozone layer. We have that eroding ozone layer on the basis of what ozone-eroding substances have already made their way up into the atmosphere. That does not count all the CFCs, or chlorofluorocarbons, that are already on the earth's surface at this point in the form of discarded styrofoam cups, discarded or still in use refrigerators, foam cushions, waste solvents, or whatever, and which have yet to make their way up to the point where they pose a threat to the ozone layer. Even if we were to stop the production of these substances today, we would still have a much more serious problem than we have today with ozone layer erosion because, whether we like it or not, all these substances which have not yet made their way to the ozone layer will in fact make their way to the ozone layer eventually.
I think it becomes a matter of not just a technological but a moral urgency. These are the type of questions that test whether or not we have any sense of what I would call intergenerational morality, whether or not for short term, practical or, as in the case of the Hon. Member for Selkirk- Interlake, ideological goals we will put off, retard or not promote as much as we should urgent activity with respect to finding a solution to this problem.
Every time we use one of these substances in whatever way that we use them, we are in fact, to the extent that it could be avoided, putting our own personal material convenience ahead of the welfare of people who will come after us, particularly those who may be more vulnerable than most to diseases such as skin cancer. The primary worry is about increased levels of skin cancer. This is what one thinks about when one thinks about the erosion of the ozone layer and the health problems associated with it.
I just wanted to get those points across, especially with respect to the sense of urgency, because it does not appear urgent and, yet it is. It is extremely hard to get people excited about the fact that over the Antarctic there is a hole developing in the ozone layer. But the fact is that the ozone layer problem is not just with respect to the hole in the ozone layer over the Antarctic but it also has to do with the thinning of the ozone everywhere. It is countries such as Canada and people such as Canadians in the northern hemisphere who are most vulnerable to the effects of a thinned ozone layer. It is precisely for that reason that Canada should not only be showing the leadership that it has been but should be showing even more leadership. That will mean making some tough decisions with respect to what I would call environmental substance abuse.
I have mentioned in the House before that we continue to contribute to the problem here ourselves by virtue of the fact that we churn out every day I do not know how many styrofoam cups in this place, in committees and in the House. Everyone is guilty of it. At some of the churches that I have
been at one would think that the styrofoam cup is a sacramental object. One cannot escape it. Yet the styrofoam cups which are needlessly being produced and used are not disappearing. They are going somewhere. Somewhere there could be a mountain of styrofoam cups, if we could get them all together. That would be offensive enough in terms of producing useless garbage. But the fact of the matter is that when this useless garbage finally breaks down it releases these CFCs which eventually accumulate at the level of the ozone layer and have the effect of destroying the ozone.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and I say it as one who, when I need a cup of coffee around here, uses one of those styrofoam cups myself, so I do not say this self-righteously, that it is a perfect example of how we cannot rely on individual decisions if we want to be environmentally responsible. We have to change the structures. We have to change the products. We have to change the things which are available to people and the choices which are available to them, even if that means restricting choices that are available.
I think we should start right here in the House of Commons with respect to some of these issues. Styrofoam cups is a good place to start. I am sorry for having to bring this in but it is a pet peeve of mine and has been for some 10 years now. It just goes to show how difficult it is to make just one little change in the habits of people.
Because I see you indicating my time is soon to come to an end, Mr. Speaker, at least with respect to my speech, I wish to make a final comment with respect to the question of the environment and jobs. The Hon. Member for Selkirk- Interlake referred to this, and I am glad he did. One of the things that has always puzzled me is that in our society it is okay-I do not mean to say that I think it is okay, but it is generally accepted as being okay-that people should lose their jobs because the quarterly profit margin of some corporation is down and it needs to improve its cash flow, its credit rating, or whatever the case may be, so it has to lay off a lot of people. Or someone has bought another plant, bought out a competitor, and the most rational and efficient thing to do is to shut the plant down because it is too old.
I refer to all these excuses that are given all the time by the corporate world, and by Government for that matter, for shutting down plants and laying off people and getting rid of jobs, because by contrast if one suggests for a moment that jobs should be lost, that substantial adjustments should be made in the economy or in any particular sector in order to save the planet, then one is told to forget it. That would be a lousy reason, according to the conventional wisdom.

I say that it is about time that we stopped putting as much priority as we do on the short-term economic goals and put more priority on long-term environmental goals. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too take pleasure in rising in this debate in support of the motion put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). The motion states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the
advisability of intensifying research for alternatives to refrigerants, such as
freon, which contain chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) that erode the earth's ozone
layer.
Chlorofluorocarbons or CFCs, as we all know by now, are used as a coolant in refrigerators, freezers, and air-conditioning units. They are also used in foam, including rigid insulation foam, flexible foam for cushions, and foam for packaging foods. The use of CFCs in aerosols, such as hair spray, was banned in 1980, but CFCs are used extensively in various consumer goods.
The threat posed by CFCs is that they erode the ozone layer in the stratosphere some 20 to 40 kilometres above the earth. Once released into the atmosphere they can last some 60 to 300 years.
As many as Canadians now know, the ozone layer acts as earth's sun screen. It blocks some of the sun's ultraviolet radiation from reaching the surface of the earth and from reaching the bodies of human beings and other animals. If ultraviolet radiation were to be increased, the health of the human species and other species would be seriously affected, as well as the environment in which we live.
As many Members who have spoken in this debate have mentioned, in September, 1987, the UNEP, the United Nations Environment Program sponsored a protocol on substances that deplete the ozone layers. This was signed in Montreal by some 24 nations and the European Economic Community. If ratified and implemented, it would reduce the global consumption of CFCs to 50 per cent of the 1986 level by 1998.
Is this reduction the limit? Certainly this reduction is important, but let us try to put it in perspective. It will partially solve the problem, but how effective will it be in solving the problem which is the depletion of the ozone layer?
Environment Canada has taken as its position that, because of the long life of CFCs in the stratosphere, some 60 to 300 years, a reduction of 85 per cent is required. The 50 per cent reduction that was agreed to in Montreal in September, 1987
Alternatives to Refrigerants
is not sufficient. A reduction of 85 per cent would be required to stabilize the levels of ozone in the atmosphere, that is, to ensure that there would be no increase above the levels that are currently present. This view is endorsed by many environmental groups and organizations that advocate the complete elimination as soon as possible.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport, in his remarks in the House emphasized that there is a role for Government, for industry, and for consumers in fighting this question and in trying to seek a reduction and an elimination of the release of CFCs into the atmosphere. Consumers can reduce consumption of products which contain CFCs. There has been considerable public concern for this issue.
Recently, Provigo, a leading grocery chain in Quebec, announced that it would be eliminating the use of packaging which contains CFCs or which release CFCs into the atmosphere. That is an indication that industry will respond to consumer demand and that it is prepared to play a role in this question. The Government could help the consumer make an informed choice by introducing labelling requirements to identify products that contain CFCs.
In addition to that, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport, asked the Government to go beyond the protocol that was signed last September. He asked the Government to ratify the protocol immediately, but also to develop a strategy to reduce the consumption of CFCs to zero, and to launch a global initiative with like-minded Governments to eliminate completely ozone depleting CFCs.
With respect to the particular motion before us, you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Member urged or asked that the Government consider the advisability of intensifying research for alternatives to refrigerants that contain CFCs. This motion was selected by a committee of this House for debate over a five-hour period.
I found it quite remarkable that the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) who spoke earlier this afternoon questioned why the Member for Davenport even brought forward this motion. He stated that the Government was doing all it can and there is really no need to debate this issue. In reply to the Member for Selkirk-Interlake, I would remind him that this motion was selected by a committee of our peers in this House for debate, because they considered it important enough to merit the attention of all Members of this House. They considered it important enough to be debated during Private Members' hour for a five-hour period, at which point there will be a vote on this motion.
In his comments in the House the Hon. Member for Davenport urged that the Government intensify research for non-CFC solutions in a number of areas. Without repeating his suggestions, I urge other Members who participate in the debate to read those suggestions and to try to engage in some kind of constructive debate on his various proposals.

It would seem that this is an ideal opportunity for Hon. Members to make themselves aware of the kind of research which is being conducted in this field. Perhaps they could request the Library of Parliament or the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) to provide us with some kind of status report so that we can see what is happening in industry and in government labs and what kind of money is being spent in Canada on researching this issue. Then we could try to compare what we are doing in Canada with what is being done in other countries. I think we all know that a major challenge which we face in Canada is the need to increase our capacity for research.
In conclusion let me indicate that we lack an industrial research base. Very little research and development is conducted in Canada. If there were one area in which Canadians could make a contribution, certainly it would be in ensuring that our industry develops a capacity for producing manufacturing equipment and products which respect our northern environment. Certainly there is an increasing demand in the world for environmentally sound products and manufacturing processes.
The motion of the Hon. Member for Davenport provides opportunity for Members of Parliament to inquire about the state of industrial and governmental research on this subject. subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext:
As someone pointed out earlier, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) is urging the Government to consider the advisability of intensifying research for alternatives to substances which harm the ozone layer. Substitute products and technologies play an important role in any effort designed to reduce our dependency on chemicals which adversely affect the ozone layer. The solution to the international problem created by such chemicals depends on these products and technologies.
Mr. Speaker, the Government is fully aware of these facts. After all, if there were no substitute products which are harmless to the environment our society would have to make a decision: to protect the ozone layer, or to go on using a number of products which are absolutely essential to the health and well-being of mankind. Were we forced to make this kind of decision, Mr. Speaker, our efforts to implement programs to protect the ozone layer against the harmful effects of chemical products would be severely curtailed. Indeed it would be tantamount to an unfortunate backward step after the progress recorded in Montreal last September.
Adoption of the Montreal protocol concerning substances which are harmful to the ozone layer is an unmistakable reminder to industry that time has come to find substitutes for chlorofluorocarbons and halons. Fully aware of the trade benefits which will flow from the development of substitute
products which are harmless to the environment, the industrial sector will live up to the challenge. Extensive research and development projects are already under way concerning major uses for such products as plastic foams, cooling fluids, substances used in portable air conditioning units and fire extinguishers, sterilizers and cleaning solvents. The public sector has been involved in many aspects of these projects. Mr. Speaker, I would simply give a few examples to the House.
First of all, as mentioned earlier, the Federal Government, together with the Environmental Protection Agency and the Conservation Foundation of the United States, sponsored in Washington, from January 13 to 15, a technical conference on alternative substances. On this occasion, producers and users of these substances, as well as scientists and representatives of regulatory agencies, shared the most recent technical developments on these substances and their marketing.
Also, we continue to promote the use, whenever possible, of alternative substances and technologies which are not detrimental to the environment, in order to reduce the demand for the CFCs and halons, hence their consumption. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the Federal Government intends also to show leadership in making sure not to indirectly create obstacles to the marketing of alternative products and technologies. We intend therefore to reduce as much as possible in our codes and standards the requirements for CFCs and specific halons.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize that the development and marketing of alternative subtances and technologies are only one element in our fight to protect the ozone layer from harmful effects. The Government is determined to assume the responsibilities described in the Montreal Protocol towards future generations and the international community. In this connection, in Canada we have initiated a series of activities. I should like to describe briefly some of these activities.
First of all, we have started to determine the various ways to reduce CFCs and halons consumption. Later on, we shall examine each of the options from the view point of cost and benefits to our society. Meanwhile, we shall consult the interested parties, the so-called interests. Clearly, Mr. Speaker, the result of cost-benefit analysis will vary greatly depending on whether there are alternatives to the substances which harm the earth's ozone layer.
Also, we have initiated a major study in the industry in order to determine the levels of production, use and sale of the CFCs, halons and substances containing them. By repeating this study each year, we will be able to monitor market development, the effectiveness of regulatory legislation, as well as determine the effects of alternative substances and technologies available on the market.
Finally, we should not overlook the fact that science should greatly contribute to the solution of the thinning of the ozone layer problem. Mr. Speaker, by allowing the implementation of stringent regulatory measures at the international level, should it become necessary on the basis of scientific data to
March 8, 1988

prevent further depletion of the ozone layer the Montreal Protocol provides that solution.
As to the ozone layer itself, control and research activities, which of necessity are international in scope, are coordinated by the World Meteorological Organization, the United Nations Environment Program, and the International Commission on Ozone, which comes under the International Council of Scientific Unions. In Canada, there are ozone layer control stations in Toronto, Edmonton, Churchill, Goose Bay and Resolute Bay. Measurements are taken every week from these stations, except the one in Toronto. We are thus making a substantial contribution to the world network for monitoring the ozone layer, which consists of 94 stations, 21 of whom are measuring regularly. The network's activities are coordinated by the WMO. Canada also operates the World Ozone Data Centre for the WMO, and we are responsible for archiving and publishing ozone data from all parts of the world.
Although measuring is now done by satellite, data collected by land-based stations provide a set of basic historical data that are essential in determining how the ozone layer evolves. For more than forty years measurements were taken with a Dobson spectrophotometer, but laboratories at Environment Canada have now developed a new instrument, the Brewer spectrophotometer, which can measure ozone and sulphur dioxide concentrations automatically and also more accurately than was the case before. The Brewer instruments are manufactured by Sci-Tec in Saskatoon, which has sold orders in Sweden, Germany, Belgium and Greece.
On the space shuttle's 41-G Mission, Marc Garneau, the first Canadian astronaut, took along equipment to measure the ozone layer with the help of a solar photometer. The data collected by Mr. Garneau are now being analyzed to establish profiles of ozone, water vapour and aerosol concentrations and to compare these with measurements taken by instruments on board satellites, instruments that cannot be calibrated directly.
Canadian scientists regularly participate in NASA experiments concerning the stratosphere. Many of these experiments involve measuring trace-constituents from large stratospheric balloons that go up to altitudes of 30 to 35 kilometres and from rockets that go up as far as 50 kilometres.
In short, Mr. Speaker, Canadians can be proud of their scientists who are making an important contribution to world research on the ozone layer.
Mr. Speaker, I hope I have been able to shed some light on the very substantial efforts being deployed in the public and private sectors to develop substitutes for CFCs and halons and to make these available as soon as possible. In concluding, I would like to mention that Environment Canada will continue to work very closely with the research and development sector, and that if certain aspects require additional support, the Government will do everything in its power to provide that support.
