Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to join in the debate today. I want to emphasize the importance this Government places on the acute problem of ozone depletion now before us, and the longer term, more chronic problem of man-induced climate change.
I find it interesting to hear today that the Canadian Government has outlined several activities it has embarked upon and some of the support it has had. It is important that we recognize the issues and recognize that the private sector has been involved. Self-interest and concern about the environment are prompting chemical companies to develop compounds as commercial alternatives to chlorofluorocarbons. An article in The Financial Post outlined that in the private sector there is a great deal of involvement by chemical companies which realize the days of widespread use of CFCs are numbered. There are two choices. Either lose a relatively small but lucrative market, or come up with a safer chemical. Clearly companies are coming up with safer chemicals. This approach will help us all. If the market-driven forces can come up with new approaches and give safety to Canadians, then we will all be in a much better shape.
We have to ask ourselves a series of questions in order to form an opinion on this motion. For example, what needs to be done globally to design and implement comprehensive remedial measures to address this issue? What role should Canada continue or start to play internationally that is consistent with our resource capabilities and expertise? What should Canada do domestically to meet the requirements of the Montreal protocol? What can we do domestically in a regulatory sense to go beyond the protocol in order to serve as a role model? How do we facilitate the orderly transition away from these ozone depleting substances so as to avoid any unnecessary unemployment or other social upheavals? How can we work constructively with industry and environmental groups to achieve the previous point? What role can the Canadian Government play domestically and internationally to facilitate the required technology transfer? What research is currently ongoing in what areas? Is it enough? Can it be better co-ordinated or focused? What role can or should the Canadian Government play in the global research effort, taking into account our contributions to the previous points?
In the introduction to my speech I said that the Canadian Government has taken this into account and has provided an environment in our country where private sector companies, as mentioned in The Financial Post report of February 12, 1988, would come forward. I believe that 12 companies now, Canadian companies in the main, have come forward and spoken about sales in the CFC area of $50 million. These sales would provide jobs for Canadians and the forefront of the research and development would help future generations of Canadians. In fact, we feel that over $10 million would be put into research alone in one group for this effort. There is no

March 8, 1988
Alternatives to Refrigerants
other sharing of information because the companies are still competing, trying to be the first with the appropriate alternatives and with commercializing them.
This is a very important issue to which the private sector is responding and which we think will be in the best interests of Canadians. The Government has not shirked its responsibility. In fact, Environment Canada officials have just returned from an informal meeting in Paris where strategic discussions took place on the various ways and means of encouraging the earliest possible entry into force date for both the Vienna Convention and the Montreal protocol. To date, 16 countries have ratified the Vienna Convention and three more are expected to ratify it very shortly. The Vienna Convention must enter into force before the Montreal protocol can be brought into being.
There is another reason that the entry into force of this convention is important, notably, the convention's subsidiary requirement to adopt programs for research, systematic observations, scientific and technological co-operation, exchange of information and technological transfer. The entry into force of the convention should create an enhanced focus on a global scale on the research activities into these substitutes.
The Montreal protocol requires 11 ratifications. We expect that these criteria will be met sometime this year, 1988. However, our concern is that we must have all of the world's major producers and consumers ratified to feel secure in the knowledge that the problem has been truly harnessed and a meaningful solution is clearly in the process of implementation.
Let us focus on what role Canada should play in the ongoing research efforts to find environmentally acceptable alternatives for the ozone-depleting substances. Since the early 1970s when concern was first raised about CFCs, the producers of CFCs have been searching for environmentally acceptable alternatives. I have spoken about the growth of research and development in the private sector in this industry by Canadian firms. They have been eager, worked ahead and are truly finding substitutes and alternatives. They have produced some new chemicals that have appeared to be more environmentally acceptable. At this stage they are working on their commercial viability.
This spark of industrial research interest seemed to go through stages where it was on a downturn between 1980 and 1985. With the Vienna Convention and the Montreal protocol this has encouraged research to such an extent that it is now carrying on at an unprecedented rate. We recognize that the same expensive toxicity testing will be required globally. Many of the world's CFC producers have joined in a co-operative research program worth about $8 million. The work will focus predominantly on HCFC 123 and HCFC 134A. These are promising candidates to replace CFCs in refrigeration and other major applications. These chemicals contain a hydrogen atom, are therefore less stable and consequently have little or
no ozone layer-depleting potential. The industry expects that this testing program will take about five years, but we are hopeful that it can be completed sooner.
The depth of the research and development of new products and materials shows that the Government is interested in cooperating not just with the Canadian industry but globally with all the companies of the world. We are focusing on this problem and we think that research and development will bode well for the future of Canadians. All the citizens of the world can rest a little easier tonight knowing that this Government, the people of Canada and the top young researchers of Canada are eagerly working within the private sector as well as through government initiatives to ensure that we can work together to defeat this problem which affects our future.
It is good to see Canada in a leadership role in this scientific research and development. We are playing our part and paying our dues. Because we are one of the most scientifically educated nations in the world, our young people have the ideas, the foresight and, above all, the drive and desire to participate in the solving of the world's problems. The ozone problem is clearly one of the major scientific problems that must be addressed. I am very proud that young Canadians have come forward to show the Canadian flag to the world. We indeed will be part of the solution. These new substitutes will enhance our viability and we are just delighted to be involved with that.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be involved in this debate today. I would like to thank my colleagues who have spoken before me for the number of points they have made on this private Member's motion.
The motion is certainly one that, at first blush, all Hon. Members would find generally supportable. Upon further examination, however, I fear that the motion only covers one very small part of what is a major issue facing not only the environmental community but indeed all Canadians.
The motion calls for the Government to consider the advisability of intensifying research for alternatives to refrigerants such as freon which contain chlorofluorocarbons, CFCs, that erode the earth's ozone layer. Indeed, we have heard a number of Hon. Members speak, not only today but in past debates on this motion, and I think they have touched on many good points.
Obviously, whenever one jumps in or out of an air-conditioned vehicle or building, one does not stop to try to understand the way refrigerant coolants work. Certainly few people give serious enough consideration to the impact on the ozone layer and indeed the environment generally of the generically-named chlorofluorocarbons or CFCs.
In closing off this hour of debate tonight, I would like to paraphrase briefly a number of points my colleagues have
March 8, 1988

made. We heard of many of the major events that led up to the Vienna Convention for the protection of the ozone layer and the Montreal protocol. My colleague from London just now spoke eloquently of the role Canada has played in the development of these conventions and protocols and how we are working on international institutional mechanisms that will be in place on a global scale, as well as dealt with the domestic treatment of CFCs.
It has also been pointed out tonight that the need for scientific research is imperative. This need is probably exceeded only by the need for not only Canada but many of the countries of the world to recognize that shortsightedness and narrow self-interest will imperil all of us. The matter should be dealt with appropriately.
We recall the highlights of the conference co-sponsored by Environment Canada held in Washington in January. This conference was important because it identified concretely that there is a tremendous level of activity in the private sector to share research information and to initiate joint programs. As well, there is a sharing of information on current technologies designed to reduce CFCs and halons. Some of these initiatives include substitute chemicals, recycling, recovery and destruction.
The conference showed that producers, researchers, regulators, environmental groups and even the media are discussing the status of the development of product substitutes and alternative processes. Things are moving forward. A platform was also provided at the Washington conference for industry to report on its progress to date, a key element which goes to the heart of the motion that is before us today.
In debate, Hon. Members have talked about the unprecedented level of research that has been done. Research is moving forward on several fronts. We are clearly faced with an environmental problem caused by our ever-growing dependence on so-called halons and CFCs which are currently used in what many consider to be essential uses.
We have identified in a general way the Government's intention to address the obligations in the protocol arising from the Vienna Conference. Our Government has spoken very directly about continuing research efforts to find suitable alternative chemicals. We have pointed out that there are many hurdles remaining. We have discussed the products and the services, the technologies we now need to ensure that there is an orderly transition to more environmentally suitable products.
The Government has attempted to provide Hon. Members in this debate with a sense of our action plan and our timetable for meeting the mandated global reduction requirements for CFCs and halons. We have indicated that we are now doing several things. We are preparing for ratification of the Montreal protocol. We are preparing a comprehensive control options report. As well, we are collecting data to determine the cost benefits and the potential dislocations associated with each of the options to which I have referred. We have stated
Adjournment Debate
on numerous occasions that we need the Canadian environmental protection Act, not just to ratify the Montreal protocol but also to implement many of the control actions that will be taken.
In respect of the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), the message of this Government is clear. There are many things that Government, industry, consumers and indeed all Canadians can and should be doing to remedy the ozone-depletion problem. Every participant in this issue should play a role to some extent.
Industry has an important responsibility, and I have mentioned thus far many of the actions internationally and domestically that the Government has taken. I want to end off this evening by touching briefly on the role of industry.
Because of the market-driven nature of this issue, we have seen the industry has what could only be called a foot race. This foot race involves the development and the technological advancement of alternatives to CFCs. In The Globe and Mail of February, just over a month ago, there was an article entitled "CFC replacement produced". It was a short piece which talked about the work of the Dupont chemical company in developing research in CFC alternatives at its New Jersey plant as well as in Canada.
While it is important that Government continue the work we are undertaking, I think this motion does not go far enough in saying what industry and indeed all Canadians can do.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-DISPATCH OF PARLIAMENTARY MISSION TO HAITI-CONDITIONS/QUERY WHETHER ARRANGEMENTS MADE TO HOLD TRULY DEMOCRATIC ELECTIONS IN HAITI

Mr. Speaker, on February 2 last, I asked the Government whether it was judicious to send a delegation of Canadian parliamentarians to Haiti.
I received then rather vague answers that, I must say, resemble the position of the Canadian Government towards a country that unfortunately has been through very tragic events.
However, I would like now, a month later, to report on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada on the work of the Group of parliamentarians responsible for examining Canada's relations with Haiti. I wish first to thank the officials of the Department of External Affairs and the Canadian International Development Agency for the very useful information they provided us at the briefing meetings we had in Ottawa, which I found not only instructive but quite thorough. We greatly appreciated their willingness to help and most of all their candour.
I would also like to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary of the Minister for the way he chaired the public hearings in Montreal, on February 16, 17 and 18 last. I was very happy with the calibre and diversity of the submissions we received. I am convinced we should take them into consideration when we draft our report to the Minister.
Earlier this week, the Government published a statement confirming the visit of the Group of paliamentarians to Haiti next week.
The fourth paragraph of the statement says the following:
During their visit to Haiti, Canadian parliamentarians will have an opportunity to meet with representatives of the new Haitian Government, unions, business communities, members of organizations for the protection of human rights. They will also have the opportunity to visit aid projects in and outside the capital of Port-au-Prince and to discuss with the beneficiaries of those programs.
They will also contact members of the Canadian community in Haiti, as well as representatives of international organizations and other countries maintaining relations with Haiti.
It is on the strenght of that program that we think our visit to Haiti will be useful. I will therefore be happy to join that delegation where I will represent the Liberal Party of Canada.
We fully realize that we cannot rewrite recent Haitian history. We believe that the Haitian people were ready for democracy but that bloody events have clouded the issue. While recognizing that Mr. Leslie Manigat has come to power in rather special circumstances, we cannot in all fairness hold him responsible for the incidents that happened at the end of 87.
As a witness was saying in Montreal last month, and I quote,
The record of new President Leslie Manigat speaks in his favor and gives the people some hope as to his competence. However, we must be aware of the
political and economic context in which the new President will assume his
duties.
I must also say that the electoral program of Mr. Manigat's political organization, which was sent to us and which I reviewed very carefully, is very impressive. And surely if Haiti can implement that program, the Haitian people will benefit substantially.
Therefore, I hope to hold frank discussions with both government and opposition representatives during my stay in Port-au-Prince. However, I would be greatly disappointed if our parliamentry delegation was unable to meet with the President himself to discuss frankly and informally with him his intentions concerning the enforcement of the Constitution which has been readily and massively supported by the Haitian people. That new Constitution prescribes some duties to the government and we hope that the new President will comply with them.
Secondly, we will have to inquire directly to the president, the prime minister and senior ministers about Canadian aid. We have been advised by party representatives that the new President disapproved of the proliferation of non-governmental organizations. Yet, a very high percentage is not vitually all of the Canadian aid to Haiti goes through non-governmental organizations and surely if this type of aid is not welcomed, the nature of Canadian aid in that country could be substantially altered.
Finally, in closing I should like to ask this government what are its intentions concerning the enforcement of human rights. Unquestionably, the bloody events of last year were absolutely unfortunate, those responsible of such incidents must be brought before the courts and justice must be done. And it would be interesting and even important to learn from the President himself what he intends to do about that.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Clinch (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as announced yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the parliamentary group responsible for looking at relations between Canada and Haiti will visit Haiti from March 13 to 18, 1988.
After the installation of the new Haiti Government on February 12, our Embassy had an opportunity to discuss with the authorities in charge the details of the group's visit. The Haitian authorities have requested a slight postponement, to have more time to ready themselves and to sift through their outstanding business. In turn, the Embassy will arrange meetings of parliamentarians with various non-governmental groups, such as representatives of the opposition, churches, labour unions, business groups, human rights organizations. Members of the group also will have an opportunity to visit aid projects, to meet members of the Canadian community and representatives of international organizations and other countries active in Haiti.
March 8, 1988

This is therefore a major program that should allow the group to proceed with the completion of their mandate. The latter essentially is to observe the situation in Haiti on the aftermath of the January 17 elections, as well as the mechanics of Canadian co-operation, in order to determine how Canada's relations with Haiti can best be organized to meet the Haitian needs and aspirations, including their desire for a better democratic life.
In fulfilling its mandate, the group will be careful to respect Haiti's internal sovereignty and resist pressures that might lead it to launch into investigations beyond its terms of reference.
In conclusion, I would like to point out there is every appearance that the parliamentary group will visit Haiti in a period of significant calm, after two years of political turmoil in that country. The new Haitian Government seems to be enjoying favourable conditions to put in place the elements that will allow it to implement its political agenda, but considering the challenges of economic development and prevailing social divisions in Haiti it presumably will not enjoy a long respite. In that context, the comments and recommendations the parliamentary group may want to share with us will rapidly face the test of reality.

Over the last few months and years, Mr. Speaker, I have told you a number of stories. I wonder if I have ever told you the story of the Canadian who went to visit the United States. He travelled to Windsor, drove across the border and up to the U.S. Immigration Customs official. The official, of course, asked him the standard question: "Where were you born?". His answer was: "Toron-na". That is the way we refer to Toronto in our city. The next question was: "Where are you going?" He said he was going to Detroit. The officer then asked: "Are you carrying a gun?" This particular person was taken aback but he said, no, of course not. The officer reached in his pocket and said: "Here, take mine, because if you are going to Detroit, you will need it".
I do know whether or not you thought that was a humorous story, Mr. Speaker. It was intended to be a little humorous, but it is an illustration of a tragic fact. It is tragic that someone might even consider that one should need a gun if one went to visit Detroit or, indeed, many other places in the United States. I think there are a number of Canadians and other people who feel that that in fact is the case, that it would be essential. They feel that because, after all, some of the crime statistics in the United States are frightening.
For instance, in 1985 in the City of Chicago, which is somewhat comparable in size to the City of Toronto, there were 666 murders as compared to only 61 murders in Toronto.
Adjournment Debate
In 1985 in the City of Houston, which is comparable to your city, Mr. Speaker, Montreal, there were 457 murders compared to only 81 in Montreal.
In Washington, D.C. which is comparable to the City of Calgary, there were 147 murders as compared to 16 in Calgary. Milwaukee is roughly about the same size as Winnipeg. It had 68 murders as compared to 16 in Winnipeg. Jacksonville, Florida, is roughly the same size as Edmonton, Alberta. It had some 90 murders in 1985 compared to only 19 in Edmonton.
When I mention Jacksonville, Florida, immediately comes to my mind the fact that last year the State of Florida passed some new gun laws. It passed something called the Concealed Weapons Licensing Act. That particular Act did not in any way restrict the use of or the carrying of hand guns. In fact, it did not control hand guns in any way. What it did was allow all the citizens of Florida to carry hand guns. That is exactly the opposite to some sort of gun-control law. Now everyone in the State of Florida can carry a hand gun, the taxi driver, the local butcher, the baker or candlestick maker. Any of them under this legislation can carry a hand gun, a colt, a magnum, a barretta, you name it, Mr. Speaker, they are all quite legal now in the State of Florida.
I know that the United States Rifle Association thinks that is probably a good idea. After all, it is consistent with the American Constitutional right to bear arms and it is consistent with the concept of fighting crime, I suppose. I suspect at the same time there are many Canadians who would agree with that and who feel that the Florida gun law was probably quite appropriate. Perhaps you do, Mr. Speaker, although I hope not. I am glad to see you shaking your head, Mr. Speaker.
However, there are as you know, Mr. Speaker, rural Canadians, hunters, those in gun clubs-perhaps even the Parliamentary Secretary is a hunter, I do not know, although we will be hearing from him in a minute-who feel that we do not need stricter gun control laws. I was speaking to the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) yesterday and when he heard the mention of gun control laws, his hair stood on end. He was shocked by the very thought.
However, my constituents, at least most of them, being urban constituents feel very strongly that we need some stricter gun control laws in Canada. They feel that way because they know that the police say that there is actually a direct link between the availability of guns and the number of people who get killed or injured each year. They recall and in fact become jittery when they think of the fact that last August Canada Customs seized a shipment of more than 900-more than 900-fully automatic light and heavy machine guns that were bound for Calgary.
These things disturb me, and they disturb my constituents. That is why back on October 14, 1986-not 1987 but 1986-I asked the Minister if he intended to further tighten up our gun

March 8, 1988
Adjournment Debate
control laws and when we could expect this. The Minister's answer at that time, back in October of 1986, was that we could expect those new gun control laws "shortly".
Time passed and in November of 1987, over one year later, I again asked the Minister in the House when was "shortly". What was the Minister's reply? The Minister replied that shortly is soon.
A little later than that, in October of last year, Mr. Nick Austin, who is one of the chief bureaucrats in charge of gun control legislation, was quoted in the newspapers as saying that we could expect gun control legislation to come in before the end of the year. That was 1987. However, he said that more likely it would be "early" in the new year. That was 1988. We are now into March, getting close to being a little later than early.
Tonight I want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary if he can tell my constituents, and Canadians, how shortly is shortly? How soon is soon? How early is early? I hope that we will get a response from the Government to indicate that we will get some action on this matter, and get some action quickly. I would hate to have the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) have to return to the House as a Minister in order to get some action on gun control laws.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard Grise (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure my colleague, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway), that I do not even own a pellet gun. So, he can rest assured in that respect.
Gun control has a long history in Canada. It has been supported by successive Governments. In fact, the first nationwide permit system respecting hand guns was introduced in the 1892 Criminal Code. The strict control of hand guns has been a fundamental principle of Canada's gun control program.
As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) assured the House in a statement on November 3, 1987, the Government does not intend to emulate the State of Florida by relaxing the control of hand guns.

Mr. Speaker, Parliament made major changes to the firearm legislative provisions in its 1977 legislation amending the Criminal Code. Following the implementation of these provisions in 1979, an independant assessment carried out over a three year period brought to light positive changes in the use of firearms and the sentences imposed in criminal matters. For instance, murders committed with firearms as a percentage of all murders are considerably down. The 1986 statistics on homicides published recently by Statistics Canada also demonstrate that Canada's legislative provisions have a positive effect since the proportion of homicides committed with firearms went down from nearly 40 per cent in 1976 to 30,8 per cent in 1986.
The Statistics Canada report also indicates that in 1986, the number of offenses committed with handguns was considerably down compared to the total number of offenses committed with firearms. It went down from an average of 29.3 per cent over the past ten years to 21.7 per cent. In 1986, 39 homicides were committed with handguns in Canada compared with 10,000 in the United States. In other words, the number of murders committed with handguns is 25 times greater in the United States than in Canada, taking into account our respective populations.
As the Minister of Justice has previously indicated, a process of ongoing review and extensive consultations are continuing to identify where amendments to the firearms legislation might be appropriate. However, substantial shifts in the direction of Canada's gun laws are not contemplated.
The Government favours a balanced approach which recognizes the legitimate interests of firearms users and the needs of public safety. In seeking to strike an appropriate balance, the Government has welcomed representations from all those groups and individuals affected by the legislation, and federal and provincial officials have maintained a close collaboration.
At this moment, Mr. Speaker, available evidence suggests that there is no need for changes to Canada's firearms legislation.
In closing, if at any time the Hon. Member for York East has the intention of looking at the application and supervision of the law in Florida, and if he wishes to visit Miami, I will fully support and offer my service to join with him in his visit and to see that in Miami there is not only vice but there is something nice too.
NATIONAL REVENUE-NORTHERN TAX ALLOWANCES- REQUEST THAT REGULATIONS BE AMENDED/APPLICATION OF AMENDMENTS

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity today to interrogate the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Grise) on the northern tax allowance. I am also a little regretful in that the answer given to me on February 23 when I raised this matter in the House was not that far from satisfactory, and certainly better to receive than some that loosely pass for answers in this place.
Yet it is a matter I have no alternative but to pursue, because the way in which the regulations for the northern residents tax allowance have been framed set up major inequities between neighbouring communities in many parts of the country, although most of the examples that I use will be from my riding.
On a seemingly arbitrary basis some communities which are as isolated and remote, or more isolated and more remote than
March 8, 1988

some of their neighbours, appear to be excluded, while others have been accepted for a tax provision that I think I can say in a non-partisan way is a relatively generous recognition of some of the problems faced in day-to-day living by residents who live in remote and northern areas of our great country.
The Minister did indeed acknowledge in his response that there are some anomalies in the legislation. He noted that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will soon be appointing a committee to explore some of the difficulties that may exist. Last Friday, the Minister of Finance again used the word "soon", which brings up a theme that my colleague, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway), was expounding on to very good effect. We now have a movement in northwestern Ontario to ask the Government to introduce some equity into this whole situation. Mr. Michael Powers, Mayor of Geraldton and President of Northern Ontario Municipal Association, has asked the Minister for a meeting, as have the presidents of the Thunder Bay Municipal Association and the Kenora District Municipal Association, Wendy Bell and Sandra Walkey respectively, as well as Dick Lyons, Mayor of Fort Frances, and George Boissenault, Mayor of Dryden. These community leaders are concerned about not only the equity of the situation but the effect on their tax base when, by the operation of these distinctions, essentially their residents are being offered a premium of up to $60 per week, in some cases, to move just outside the boundaries of their communities and thus undercut the tax base of the community providing the services.
I should like to refer to some brief examples. Kenora, a principal town in my riding, is too close to Winnipeg to qualify. Vermilion Bay, a much smaller town of some 700 people, 90 kilometres from Kenora, is judged too close to Kenora. Dryden, 140 kilometres from Kenora, is judged too close to Kenora. Yet, when we get to Wabigoon, just 15 kilometres from Dryden, it is judged to be an isolated community. Dinorwic, just 6 kilometres down the road from Wabigoon, does not appear on the list of excluded or included communities. Borups Corners, a hamlet of some 30 people, is absent from either list. Ignace, surely one of the most isolated towns in northwestern Ontario although it is on the Trans-Canada Highway, is judged to be too close to Thunder Bay.
Similarly down in Rainy River, Fort Frances, the major community, is excluded but communities to the west, to the east, and to the north of Fort Frances are all judged to be eligible. Nestor Falls, whose students face the longest bus ride anywhere in North America to get to high school, is also excluded, as is its neighbour, Sioux Narrows, another community which falls to about 300 people in the winter-time. Both these communities have the majority of their adult residents- and I think it is somewhere in the 80 per cent range-signing petitions against this inequitable application.
My constituents and many other Canadians in remote communities want to know if the operations of the Minister's committee will be open to the public, if the conclusions will be
Adjournment Debate
retroactive, and primarily, of course, if the communities I have listed, as the Minister asked me to, in letters to him last Monday and Tuesday will be admitted to the operation of the northern residents' tax allowance.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard Grise (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious question on a very serious issue to which I will try to reply in the few minutes I have left, because the Sergeant-at-Arms is on a very strict schedule.
For several years before 1986, some fortunate people benefitted from special tax privileges granted to the residents of isolated areas. They had the good fortune of working for corporations or businesses that were able to give their employees generous tax-exempt benefits under income tax remission orders.
When the Government introduced northern tax allowances in 1986, it marked the beginning of a new era of tax fairness for people residing in remore regions. Now not only employees but also retired people, independent workers and all taxpayers living in remote regions may ask for tax deductions to offset the high cost of living in these regions.
It is a sizeable deduction, Mr. Speaker, but more important still, it is much fairer. This legislative measure ensures that nobody becomes entitled to unduly generous tax benefits related to employment conditions in remote regions while others do not. This legislation ensures equitable tax treatment for everyone as all residents of a community designated by regulation can claim a deduction on the basis of their place of residence.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that we all agree with the concept of tax equity for the residents of remote areas. However, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) has raised the issue of tax inequity. He has vigorously stated that the list of remote communities whose residents are eligible to the deduction does not include certain communities which could be considered remote and which do not receive such tax benefits. He demands that changes be made to the list.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) has already conceded that the legislation creates anomalies in some areas. In addition, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will soon be appointing Members to a committee that will explore these anomalies with a view to fine tuning the legislation. In the interim, Mr. Speaker, you have the commitment of the Government that it will exercise compassion, sound judgment and administrative accommodation wherever possible. Across this country, employees of the tax department are routinely checking and rechecking the designation of communities to ensure fair treatment for all taxpayers.

March 8, 1988
Adjournment Debate
The Government is on the right track. We are confident that the premises of the legislation are on target. Any review of their intent will serve to show that, indeed, this Government has succeeded in bringing far greater equity to the tax system than existed previously.

I have every sympathy for people in communities adjacent to eligible communities, who may feel they are being treated unfairly. That certainly is not our intention.
You may rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that when members of Mr. Wilson's task force have completed their study and made
their conclusions known to the Government, all Canadians will be convinced we took note of their concerns and responded to their expectancies, which has always been the basic feature of this Conservative Government's policy.
